name: Ordinances from other LGUs, kept as references
note: Ordinances that provinces, cities and municipalities outside BARMM have enacted, each read in full off the LGU’s own PDF (or the Internet Archive’s copy where the LGU has taken it down). They are kept so a BARMM council can see how others drafted a code before writing its own. None of them has force in the region, and a BARMM LGU drafts under the Bangsamoro Local Governance Code (BAA No. 49), not the 1991 Local Government Code these ordinances cite. Texts read from scans by OCR carry misread words; check the original PDF before quoting one.

ordinances.title: Provincial Environmental Protection and Management Code of La Union
ordinances.shortTitle: Provincial Environmental Protection and Management Code of La Union (2002)
ordinances.summary: A provincial code that gathers La Union's environmental rules in 13 chapters: water resources, forests, air and vehicle pollution, wildlife, toxic substances, sewage, solid waste, caves, small-scale mining and mine safety. It sets rules for residents, businesses, quarry and mining operators and the cities and towns of the province, and lets the Governor issue implementing guidelines.
points: Quarry extraction needs a permit from the Provincial Governor; the quarry tax is shared 30% province, 30% city or town, 40% barangay
Bans slash-and-burn farming, cutting trees on public land without DENR clearance, and cutting coconut trees without a PCA permit and the mayor's approval
Bans smoking in cinemas, hospitals, classrooms, designated no-smoking areas and public utility vehicles; PUV drivers must carry a waste receptacle
Gold panning or sluicing needs a Bureau of Mines permit, the mayor's permit and the claim owner's written consent; minors may not be employed
Some articles, like anti-littering, apply only where the city or town has no ordinance of its own
Takes effect 30 days after approval
ordinances.penalties: Up to ₱5,000, up to 1 year in jail, or both, where no specific penalty is set
ordinances.caveat: Chapter XII, about half the text, reproduces national mine safety and health rules word for word, including their own final provisions.

barmm.verdict: Take the idea, not the text
barmm.why: Quarrying along rivers, upland clearing and small-scale mining are real pressures in BARMM, from the Lake Lanao watershed in Lanao del Sur to the rivers feeding the Liguasan Marsh in Maguindanao del Norte and del Sur. A single provincial environment code is a useful way to gather those rules. But this one is from 2003, runs 212 pages, and about half of it copies national mine safety rules, so a BARMM province should borrow its layout and a few clauses, not the text.
adopt: The quarry permit system issued by the Governor, with the quarry tax shared 30% province, 30% city or town, 40% barangay; this already matches the BLGC
The rule that articles such as anti-littering apply only where the city or town has no ordinance of its own, which avoids clashes with municipal ordinances
The ban on employing minors in gold panning and small-scale mining, and the need for the claim owner's written consent
Letting the Governor issue implementing guidelines, with a general penalty of up to ₱5,000, up to 1 year in jail, or both where no specific penalty is set
change: Re-cite quarry rules to BLGC s. 161 and s. 162: the Governor's permit covers areas of up to 5 hectares, on the mayor's recommendation, for 5 years renewable to 25; areas over 5 and up to 20 hectares go to the Bangsamoro environment ministry, not DENR
Drop Chapter XII, the copied mine safety rules, and refer to the national small-scale mining law (RA 7076) and the province's BLGC s. 512 role in regulating small-scale mining instead

Rework the slash-and-burn ban for ancestral domains: shifting cultivation by Teduray, Lambangian and Dulangan Manobo communities is customary, so consult them and the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs under BAA No. 64 and RA 8371 (IPRA) before banning it outright

Move the smoking rules out into a separate smoke-free ordinance under the national tobacco laws (RA 9211), and put solid waste rules under RA 9003 and the provincial solid waste board the province chairs under BLGC s. 512

Name the provincial environment and natural resources officer (BLGC s. 538) as the lead office, and require the sanggunian's prior approval for projects that may cause pollution or forest loss, as BLGC s. 32 does; keep penalties within the ₱5,000 and 1-year ceiling in BLGC s. 521
barmm.fits: Provinces with active quarrying, upland farming or small-scale mining: Lanao del Sur, Maguindanao del Norte, Maguindanao del Sur and Basilan.

ordinances.title: Authorizing the collection and payment of solid waste management fees in the City of Bacoor, Cavite
ordinances.shortTitle: Solid Waste Management Fees Ordinance of the City of Bacoor
ordinances.summary: Levies a yearly solid waste management fee on households and on commercial, industrial and institutional establishments in Bacoor, tiered by type, location, waste volume and floor area. The money pays for garbage collection and disposal and for the city's solid waste plan, including a materials recovery facility, a waste-to-energy plant and a bio-digester. It also lists prohibited waste practices and their penalties.
points: Sets annual fees for 37 categories, from ₱1,000 for informal settler dwellings and ₱1,500 to ₱3,000 for titled homes up to ₱300,000 for large restaurants outside malls
Private haulers pay ₱10,000 a month and transporters ₱3,000 to ₱5,000 a month
Prohibits non-segregation at source; city and barangay collectors may not pick up unsegregated waste
The city must offer free scheduled collection of bulky waste and e-waste
Late fees carry a 1% surcharge plus 1% interest a month, capped at 12% a year
Enforced by the City Environment and Service Department with the finance, assessors and permits offices
ordinances.penalties: ₱5,000 per violation; businesses face at least 30 days of permit suspension and their waste is not collected until they comply

barmm.why: Most BARMM LGUs collect garbage, if at all, from their general fund, and open dumping and burning are common in fast-growing centres like Cotabato City, Marawi, Lamitan and Bongao. A fee tied to the type and size of the generator is a fair way to pay for collection and a materials recovery facility. But Bacoor's rates and its waste-to-energy plans fit a large, well-off Cavite city, not a BARMM town.
adopt: The tiered fee idea: households, shops, institutions and industries pay by category and floor area, with a lower rate for informal settler dwellings
The 'no segregation, no collection' rule for both households and the collectors, and a duty on every barangay to set up a materials recovery facility and a hazardous waste corner
Free scheduled pick-up of bulky waste and e-waste
A list of prohibited acts that business permits can enforce, such as no colour-coded bins and dumping outside collection schedules
change: Re-cite the legal basis to BLGC s. 148 (power to create sources of revenue) and s. 21, with RA 9003 as the national law on solid waste; a fee ordinance needs public hearings first under BLGC s. 212 and full publication under s. 213, and takes effect only 15 days after publication.

Rebuild the rate table from local collection costs and incomes; ₱1,500 to ₱3,000 a year per home and ₱300,000 for a restaurant would be oppressive in most BARMM towns and open to challenge under BLGC s. 152 (no unjust, excessive or confiscatory charges).
Bacoor's 1% surcharge plus 1% monthly interest is within BLGC s. 191, but BLGC s. 153 lets the council use a Shari'ah-compliant charge instead of interest; most BARMM councils should take that route.

Drop the waste-to-energy plant. Burning municipal waste runs into the national Clean Air Act (RA 8749) and RA 9003, and it is far beyond most BARMM budgets; a composting or bio-digester facility is the realistic target.

Grade the flat ₱5,000 fine by offence and keep it within the cap: ₱5,000 or 6 months for a municipality (BLGC s. 489), ₱5,000 or 1 year for a city (s. 509). Don't leave waste uncollected as a penalty, as it ends up burned or in the river. And don't let the mayor deputise 'any resident' to collect fees, which BLGC s. 152 forbids.
barmm.fits: Cities and growing municipal centres with regular collection, such as Cotabato City, Marawi, Lamitan and Bongao; too heavy for rural towns.

ordinances.title: Ordinance instituting an engagement with the 27 barangays of Naga in the management, collection, and disposal of solid wastes; appropriating funds therefor
ordinances.shortTitle: Barangay Solid Waste Management Volunteers Ordinance of Naga City
ordinances.summary: Sets up paid barangay volunteers who help the City run waste collection, segregation and disposal in each of Naga's 27 barangays. The City Solid Waste Management Office recruits, trains and equips them with the Punong Barangays, and they serve as the office's focal persons in their barangays.
points: The City Solid Waste Management Office sets how many volunteers each barangay needs, by population, area and waste volume; current Barangay Environment Monitors get preference
Volunteers keep roads, drainage canals and waterways clean, enforce segregation and run the barangay MRF, and move residual waste to the city sanitary landfill
Volunteers are deputised to issue citation tickets for violations of city and barangay ordinances
Honoraria of ₱3,000 a month per volunteer, plus a yearly awards scheme for barangays
The Solid Waste Management Board reports yearly to the Mayor and council by the first quarter; funding starts in FY 2026

barmm.why: Many BARMM towns collect waste only in the poblacion, and garbage ends up in canals, the Rio Grande de Mindanao in Cotabato City, Lake Lanao and the shorelines of Bongao and Lamitan. Paying a few trained barangay volunteers to run segregation and the MRF is a cheap way to make the barangay share of RA 9003 work where barangays have little staff of their own.
adopt: The city or municipal waste office setting volunteer numbers per barangay by population, area and waste volume, with current barangay environment workers given preference
The volunteers' duties: clean roads and drainage, enforce segregation, run the barangay MRF and move residuals to the disposal site
A fixed monthly honorarium paid by the city or municipality, plus a yearly award for the best-performing barangays
A yearly report by the solid waste management board to the mayor and the sanggunian in the first quarter
change: Replace the RA 7160 legal basis with BLGC s. 17 (general welfare), s. 480 (the municipal solid waste management board, plan and MRF; s. 496 extends this to cities) and s. 408 (barangay segregation and MRF), with RA 9003 cited as the national law

Base the city or town paying for barangay volunteers on BLGC s. 20 (augmentation of a lower unit's service) and s. 414 (volunteer community brigades), instead of the DBM position classification manual
Check the honorarium against the Bangsamoro Civil Service Code (BAA No. 17) on engaging non-plantilla workers, and against the 45% or 55% personal services cap in BLGC s. 349

Deputising volunteers to issue citation tickets needs a written designation by the mayor and must point to a penal ordinance that already exists; volunteers are not persons in authority under BLGC s. 416, so train them and limit them to ticketing
Say when funding starts and where it sits in the budget, since Naga deferred the money to the following fiscal year
barmm.fits: Cities and larger municipalities with a working disposal site, such as Cotabato City, Marawi and Lamitan, and poblacion towns in Maguindanao del Norte and Lanao del Sur.

ordinances.title: The Gender and Development (GAD) Code of Loon, Bohol
ordinances.shortTitle: Gender and Development Code of Loon, Bohol
ordinances.summary: A comprehensive gender and development code that makes every municipal office mainstream gender in planning and budgeting and sets aside at least 5% of the budget for GAD programmes. It defines and prohibits violence, trafficking, harassment and exploitation of women and children, creates GAD bodies and support services, and sets local penalties for employers, establishments and offices that fail to comply.
points: Creates a Municipal GAD Council chaired by the Mayor (meeting at least quarterly), an Integrated Gender and Development Office under the Mayor, an inter-agency council for the protection of women and children, and a Council for Women.
At least 5% of the total budget for GAD programmes and at least 5% of the health budget for women's health; all GAD-funded plans must be reviewed and endorsed by the GAD Council.
Offers LGU employees extra maternity leave of up to 75 days (from 60) and paternity leave of up to 14 days (from 7), subject to a collective negotiation agreement.
Requires employers to provide women's seats, separate toilets, breastfeeding corners and diaper-changing stations; firms with more than 100 employees must provide reproductive health services.
Sets up a 24-hour women's desk at the PNP station, a medico-legal desk at the Municipal Health Office, barangay GAD committees and a committee on decorum and investigation.
All municipal departments must report compliance to the Sangguniang Bayan within 6 months and every 6 months after.
ordinances.penalties: Mostly a ₱2,500 fine with suspension or cancellation of business permits; national-law penalties apply to trafficking, mail-order brides (6 to 8 years and ₱8,000 to ₱20,000) and sexual harassment (1 to 6 months or ₱10,000 to ₱20,000).
ordinances.amends: Repeals or modifies all ordinances and local issuances inconsistent with it; no specific ordinance named.

barmm.why: Many BARMM LGUs already set aside the 5% GAD budget but have no code saying who plans it, who reviews it and what offices must report. Loon's code fills that gap with a council, an office and 6-month compliance reports. That matters in a region where the BLGC now treats a missing GAD plan or a misused GAD budget as grounds for discipline, and where maternal health and violence against women remain serious concerns in Lanao del Sur, the Maguindanao provinces and the island towns.
adopt: The GAD Council chaired by the mayor, meeting at least quarterly, with the rule that every GAD-funded plan is reviewed and endorsed by the council
The duty on every department to report compliance to the sanggunian within 6 months and every 6 months after
Workplace rules for employers: separate toilets, breastfeeding corners and diaper-changing stations, enforced through the business permit
The 24-hour women's desk at the police station and a medico-legal desk at the health office, which fit alongside the barangay VAW desk
change: Re-cite the 5% GAD allocation to BLGC s. 348 and add the sanctions in BLGC s. 582 (no GAD plan for 2 years, no accomplishment report or no Gender Focal Point System) and s. 584 (GAD budget used outside the plan)

Replace the integrated GAD office and the Council for Women with the Local Women's Development Officer under BLGC s. 547, whose qualifications follow Bangsamoro Women Commission guidelines (BAA No. 8), and the women's development council required by BLGC s. 130

Drop the extra maternity leave clause: 75 days is now below the 105 days that national law (RA 11210) already gives. Any extra paternity leave for LGU staff should be checked against the Bangsamoro Civil Service Code (BAA No. 17) first

Update the national-law penalties it repeats: the mail-order bride provisions it cites were replaced by RA 10906, and trafficking now runs under RA 9208 as amended. Better to refer to national law than copy penalty figures that go stale

Expect debate on the anti-discrimination section for LGBT people and on the reproductive health chapter. Councils that drop or reframe them should keep a general non-harassment clause (national law, RA 11313) and maternal health services, and consult local ulama on birth-spacing language
barmm.fits: Municipalities and cities with a functioning women's desk and health office, such as Cotabato City, Marawi, Lamitan and the larger Maguindanao towns.

ordinances.title: The Gender and Development Code of the Province of La Union
ordinances.shortTitle: Gender and Development Code of La Union
ordinances.summary: A 107-section provincial code on women's rights and gender equality, covering GAD programs, support services, political participation, work, health, education, livelihood, special sectors and violence against women and children. It creates a provincial Gender and Development Office to coordinate and monitor the code. Violations of the criminal provisions are prosecuted under national law.
points: Creates a provincial Gender and Development Office headed by a department head, with administrative, monitoring and training divisions
Creates a Pageant Regulatory Board and a task force against domestic violence
Declares March 8 of every year Provincial Women's Day and calls for a women's summit
Requires gender sensitivity orientation, registration of domestic workers and a gender-sensitive physical plan
Covers trafficking, sex trade, rape, sexual harassment, pornographic shows and surveillance of entertainment establishments
The Governor must form a committee to issue implementing rules within 60 days of publication
ordinances.penalties: No local fines; violations of Sections 57 to 70, 73, 77, 79, 80 and 91 are prosecuted under existing national laws
ordinances.caveat: The ordinance number is partly illegible in the scan; 071-2015 is taken from the source file name.

barmm.why: Provinces need one law that turns the Magna Carta of Women and the gender budget rule into offices, programs and duties, and this code does that across work, health, education, livelihood and violence. In BARMM it lands where women carry the weight of displacement in Marawi and the Maguindanao marsh towns, early marriage persists, and many LGUs still lack a working gender focal point system. The content must be reframed for a mostly Muslim region and tied to the Bangsamoro Women Commission.
adopt: The structure: a single GAD office with administrative, monitoring and training divisions that coordinates the code across offices
The chapters on support services, livelihood, political participation and special sectors (women with disabilities, older women, Indigenous women)
Referral of the criminal provisions on trafficking, rape and sexual harassment to national law instead of local fines
The 60-day deadline for implementing rules, and gender sensitivity orientation for officials and staff
change: Re-cite the legal basis from RA 7160 to BLGC s. 17 and s. 521, and build the office around the local women's development officer in BLGC s. 547, whose qualifications follow Bangsamoro Women Commission guidelines (BAA No. 8)
Tie the code's funding to the 5% GAD allocation in BLGC s. 348, and write in the sanctions BLGC s. 582 and s. 584 already set for a missing GAD plan or a misused GAD budget

Replace the domestic violence task force with the women's development council and the barangay VAW desk required by BLGC s. 130 and s. 408, and state that VAWC cases go to the courts, since BLGC s. 436 bars them from barangay settlement

Rework the reproductive health and pageant sections with the regional health ministry, the Women Commission and religious leaders; a Pageant Regulatory Board and RH definitions copied word for word will meet resistance in most BARMM towns and add little
Keep March 8 as an observance under RA 6949 (national law), not a holiday; any local holiday goes through the Chief Minister under BLGC s. 14 and BAA No. 39
barmm.fits: Provinces (Lanao del Sur, Maguindanao del Norte and del Sur, Basilan, Tawi-Tawi) and Cotabato City; municipalities should take the GAD office and services chapters only.

ordinances.title: An ordinance enacting the Gender and Development (GAD) Code of the City of Muntinlupa
ordinances.shortTitle: Gender and Development (GAD) Code of the City of Muntinlupa
ordinances.summary: Muntinlupa's GAD Code is the main basis for all city policy on gender and development. It sets gender mainstreaming duties sector by sector: education, health, environment, labour, governance, trade, peace and order, and disaster risk reduction. It creates a GAD focal point system and a permanent GAD Office, and lists prohibited acts with penalties.
points: At least 5% of the city's total annual budget goes to GAD programs, projects and services
Creates the Muntinlupa City GAD Focal Point System and a GAD Office as a regular division under the Office of the City Mayor, replacing the office created by Executive Order No. 2 of 17 January 2014
City offices and barangays must act on reports of violence against women and children within 24 hours, or face neglect-of-duty charges
Bans fund-raising that uses men or women as prizes (₱2,500 and/or 6 months) and degrading beauty contests in schools and barangays
Disclosing the identities of victims or offenders is punished by 15 days in jail or ₱2,500; degrading media content by ₱2,500 or 1 month
Sets up a Muntinlupa Council of Women, a Women's Congress every March and a city GAD Center for women in especially difficult circumstances
ordinances.penalties: ₱2,500 fines, or 15 days to 6 months in jail, for specific offences; other violations fall under national laws
ordinances.caveat: The second line of the title is illegible in the scan; the title here follows the short title in Section 1.

barmm.why: BARMM LGUs must already set aside at least 5% of their budget for gender and development and run a GAD focal point system, but many lack a code that says how the money and duties are spread across offices. Muntinlupa's code does exactly that, sector by sector, including disaster risk reduction, which matters in flood-prone towns of Maguindanao del Norte and del Sur where women carry much of the load during evacuations.
adopt: The sector-by-sector mainstreaming duties for education, health, labour, governance, peace and order and disaster risk reduction
The 24-hour deadline for city offices and barangays to act on reports of violence against women and children, with neglect-of-duty charges for failing to
The ban on fund-raising that uses women or men as prizes and on degrading beauty contests, and the ban on disclosing victims' identities
A women's council, a yearly women's congress in March and a GAD center for women in especially difficult circumstances
change: Re-cite the 5% GAD budget to BLGC s. 348, and add the BLGC's own sanctions: failing to submit the GAD Plan or set up the focal point system is dereliction of duty (s. 582), and using GAD funds outside the plan is abuse of authority (s. 584)

Replace the GAD Office under the Mayor with the Local Women's Development Officer in BLGC s. 547, whose qualifications follow Bangsamoro Women Commission guidelines (BAA No. 8); smaller municipalities should staff it within the personal services cap in BLGC s. 349

Route all VAWC reports to the barangay VAW desk (BLGC s. 408) and the police, never to the lupon: BLGC s. 436 bars amicable settlement of violence against women and their children; the basis stays national law (RA 9262 and the Magna Carta of Women)
Add articles on Moro, Indigenous and settler women, which Muntinlupa's code lacks, and link the women's council to the one BLGC s. 130 requires

Check penalties against your level: a municipality may set at most ₱5,000 or 6 months (BLGC s. 489), a barangay at most ₱3,000 (BLGC s. 419); drop the clause replacing Muntinlupa's Executive Order No. 2
barmm.fits: Cities and larger municipalities with staff for a GAD office, such as Cotabato City, Marawi and Lamitan; smaller towns can adopt it with one designated officer.

ordinances.title: Adopting the Marikina City Gender and Development Code of 2015
ordinances.shortTitle: Marikina City Gender and Development (GAD) Ordinance
ordinances.summary: This is a city gender and development code. It frames gender equality through protecting the family, and it covers gender violence, education, health, economic life, public participation and gender mainstreaming across city offices. It sets up the city's GAD focal point system, a GAD office and a GAD budget.
points: Prohibits physical, sexual, psychological and economic abuse against women, children, family members and LGBT persons.
Expands the Marikina Referral System to all victim-survivors of gender violence, with emergency shelter, medical aid and legal assistance.
Public officials who fail or refuse to help victim-survivors are held criminally and administratively liable under RA 3815, RA 6713 and RA 3019.
Reconstitutes the Marikina GAD Focal Point System with honoraria: ₱3,000 per semester for the chair, ₱2,500 per semester for ExeCom members and ₱2,000 a month for TWG members.
Creates a Marikina GAD Office with 12 positions, headed at SG-26, and funds it from the GAD budget.
The GAD budget must be at least 5% of the city's total budget appropriations.
ordinances.penalties: Penalties under the national laws (RA 9262, RA 9208, RA 7877 and others). Where none applies, a fine of up to ₱5,000, up to 1 year in jail, or both.

barmm.why: Every BARMM LGU must spend at least 5% of its budget on gender and development, and the BLGC punishes officials who skip the GAD plan or misuse the GAD budget. Many LGUs still have no working focal point system. This code is a full template for that system, with a referral path for survivors of violence, but its offices, honoraria and some of its framing need rework for BARMM.
adopt: The referral system for victim-survivors: emergency shelter, medical aid, legal help and counselling, funded from the GAD budget
The structure of the GAD focal point system: chair, executive committee and technical working group, with duties to plan, budget, monitor and report
The rule that officials who fail to help victim-survivors face administrative and criminal liability under national law
Penalties that defer to the national laws (RA 9262, RA 9208, RA 7877 and others), with a local fine only where none applies
change: Re-cite the 5% GAD budget to BLGC s. 348, and add the accountability rules: s. 582 (no GAD plan, accomplishment report or focal point system is dereliction of duty) and s. 584 (using GAD funds outside the plan is abuse of authority).

Replace the 12-position GAD office headed at SG-26 with a Local Women's Development Officer under BLGC s. 547, qualified under Bangsamoro Women Commission guidelines (BAA No. 8). Most BARMM LGUs are 4th class or lower and are capped at 55% for personal services by BLGC s. 349.
Drop or reword the honoraria for focal point members who are already LGU employees; BLGC s. 107 bars additional compensation unless a law authorises it, and auditors will question it.
Keep the residual penalty within the cap of the enacting LGU: ₱5,000 or 1 year for a city (BLGC s. 509), but ₱5,000 or 6 months for a municipality (s. 489).

Rework the family planning and education articles with local ulama and Indigenous elders, and say the code protects every person from violence. Removing protection for LGBT persons would be a bad idea, as victims are victims. If the wording is contested, frame the clause as protection for everyone regardless of who they are, rather than leave anyone out.
barmm.fits: Cities and 1st to 3rd class municipalities that can staff a GAD unit; smaller towns should take the focal point and referral parts only.

ordinances.title: Promulgating the Gender Equality and Social Inclusion (GESI) Code of 2025 of the City of San Fernando, La Union
ordinances.shortTitle: Gender Equality and Social Inclusion Code of the City of San Fernando, La Union (GESI Code)
ordinances.summary: A city code that localizes the Magna Carta of Women, the anti-VAWC and anti-trafficking laws for San Fernando. It sets gender equality and inclusion duties across governance, health, education, labour, agriculture, trade and tourism, housing, disaster response, media and sports. It also penalizes sexual harassment in public spaces and sets up a GAD Office and focal point system.
points: Sexual harassment in public spaces is graded light, medium or severe, with fines of ₱2,000, ₱3,000 or ₱5,000 plus gender sensitivity training
Creates an Anti-Sexual Harassment Desk, with barangay VAW desk persons serving as ASH Desk officers
A Pageant Regulatory Board, chaired by the Mayor, regulates beauty contests
Creates a city GAD Office headed by a department head (Salary Grade 25) and a Gender Focal Point System
At least 5% of the city's annual budget goes to the GAD agenda; departments and barangays must report compliance to the council within 1 year and every year after
Bans sex trafficking, commodification of women and pornographic displays that treat women as sex objects
ordinances.penalties: ₱2,000 to ₱5,000 plus gender sensitivity training, or up to 30 days in jail (up to 6 months for severe harassment), or both
ordinances.caveat: This copy leaves the mayor's approval date blank; the date given is the council's third-reading enactment.

barmm.why: BARMM LGUs must already spend at least 5% of their budget on gender and development and keep a Gender Focal Point System, but many have no code that says what the money is for. A GESI code that ties GAD duties to each office, from health to disaster response, gives the GAD budget a plan to follow. It also gives women who are harassed in public a local remedy, in cities like Cotabato City and Marawi and in conflict-affected towns where women carry heavy burdens.
adopt: The sector-by-sector duties for governance, health, education, labour, agriculture, trade, housing and disaster response
The Gender Focal Point System and the yearly compliance report from offices and barangays to the sanggunian
Sex-disaggregated databases of farmers, fisherfolk and entrepreneurs, and women's seats on resource management bodies
Barangay VAW desk officers serving as the anti-sexual harassment desk, so no new barangay post is needed
change: Re-cite the 5% GAD budget to BLGC s. 348, and add the sanctions in BLGC s. 582 (no GAD plan or focal point system) and s. 584 (misuse of the GAD budget)

Replace the SG 25 GAD department with a Local Women's Development Officer under BLGC s. 547, whose qualifications follow Bangsamoro Women Commission guidelines (BAA No. 8). Size the office to the personal services cap in BLGC s. 349; most BARMM towns are 4th to 6th class

Align the public-space harassment offences and fines with the Safe Spaces Act (RA 11313, national law), and keep jail terms within BLGC s. 489 (6 months for municipalities) or s. 509 (1 year for cities)

Drop the Pageant Regulatory Board. Expect strong objection to the SOGIE and reproductive health sections, so settle them early with the ulama and the Women Commission; the RH law and the Magna Carta of Women still apply as national law
Leave marriage and divorce among Muslims to the Code of Muslim Personal Laws and the Shari'ah courts, and keep VAWC cases out of barangay settlement as BLGC s. 436 requires
barmm.fits: Cities and 1st to 3rd class municipalities with a working GAD focal point system, such as Cotabato City, Marawi and Lamitan.

ordinances.title: Ordinance enacting the Revenue Code of the Province of Pangasinan
ordinances.shortTitle: 1998 Revenue Code of the Province of Pangasinan
ordinances.summary: Pangasinan's provincial revenue code governing the levy, assessment and collection of provincial taxes, fees and charges. The available pages set the provincial taxes on printing and publication, franchises, quarry resources, professions, amusements and delivery vehicles.
points: Tax on printing and publishing and on franchises: 50% of 1% of gross annual receipts
Tax on sand, gravel and other quarry resources: 10% of fair market value per cubic metre or metric ton, with permit and monthly reporting rules
Professional tax: ₱300 a year, due by 31 January; professionals in government service are exempt
Amusement tax: 30% of gross admission receipts, shared equally with the town; operas, concerts and exhibits are exempt except pop and rock concerts
Annual fixed tax of ₱500 on each delivery truck or van of liquor, soft drinks, cigarettes and other products
ordinances.penalties: Quarry violations: late reports ₱1,000 to ₱3,000 plus daily fines, missing reports ₱2,000 to ₱5,000, capped at ₱10,000; ₱2,000 per unpermitted piece of equipment
ordinances.caveat: The PDF has only the cover (dated December 11, 1998), the contents and pages 1 to 7 of 31, ending at Section 9; the fees, collection rules, penal provisions and signatures are missing.

barmm.verdict: Take the idea, not the text
barmm.why: BARMM provinces rely heavily on their national tax share and collect little of their own revenue, so a clear provincial revenue code is worth having. But this one is a 1998 fragment: only pages 1 to 7 of 31 survive, and several rates now exceed BLGC ceilings. Use it as a checklist of provincial tax bases, not as a draft.
adopt: The franchise tax at 50% of 1% of gross receipts, which matches the BLGC ceiling
The quarry tax at 10% of fair market value with the 30% province, 30% city or municipality and 40% barangay split, and the permit, delivery-receipt and monthly-report rules
A published fair market value table per cubic metre or metric ton for each quarry material, updated by ordinance
The professional tax structure: due by 31 January, with professionals employed only in government exempt
change: Cut the amusement tax from 30% to no more than 10% of gross admission receipts, still shared equally with the municipality (BLGC s. 164)
Limit the quarry tax to resources taken from public lands and public waters, as BLGC s. 162 allows; Pangasinan's version also reaches private land. Quarry permits up to 5 hectares follow BLGC s. 161

Reset the professional tax (up to ₱1,300, BLGC s. 163) and the delivery van tax (up to ₱2,200, or ₱6,600 for liquor trucks, BLGC s. 165) to the BARMM ceilings. Drop the ban on bringing in quarry materials from outside the province, which BLGC s. 156 on taxing goods in transit makes risky
Re-set the quarry fines against BLGC s. 576 on penalties for tax ordinance violations, and decide whether to use Shari'ah-compliant late-payment rules in place of interest (BLGC s. 153)
Follow the public hearing and publication rules for tax ordinances (BLGC s. 212 and s. 213): full publication for 3 days and posting on the Bangsamoro register, with effect only 15 days after
barmm.fits: Provinces such as Maguindanao del Norte, Maguindanao del Sur and Lanao del Sur; SGA municipalities may borrow only the professional tax part.

ordinances.title: Revised revenue code of the Municipality of General Trias, Province of Cavite
ordinances.shortTitle: Revenue Code of the Municipality of General Trias
ordinances.summary: The municipality's full revenue code, setting the taxes, fees and charges General Trias may collect under the Local Government Code. It covers graduated business taxes, community tax, mayor's permit and regulatory fees, service fees, rentals, garbage and parking charges, and the rules on collection, remedies and penalties. It took effect on 1 January 2003.
points: Chapters on business taxes, community tax, permit and regulatory fees, service fees, municipal charges, administration and penalties
Taxes are due within the first 20 days of January or of each quarter
Late payment carries a 25% surcharge plus interest of up to 2% a month, for no more than 36 months
Annual garbage fees for businesses by floor area, e.g. ₱500 for manufacturers up to 100 sq. m. plus ₱1 per sq. m. beyond
Includes a special levy on lands and a socialized housing tax, to be collected only once an enabling ordinance is passed
Officers of a company that violates the code are held liable, and fines do not excuse unpaid taxes
ordinances.penalties: A fine of at least ₱1,000 (the maximum is illegible in the scan), or 1 to 6 months in jail, or both
ordinances.caveat: The scan of the penal clause is partly illegible, and this copy has no signature block, only the line 'Enacted, 16 September 2002'.

barmm.verdict: Take the idea, not the text
barmm.why: Many BARMM municipalities still collect under old or partial revenue ordinances, and a complete code with business taxes, fees, charges, collection rules and remedies is what they lack. But this one is from 2002, written for a fast-urbanising Cavite town, and its rates, penalties and legal citations all predate the BLGC. Use it as a chapter checklist, not as a draft.
adopt: The chapter order: business taxes, community tax, permit and regulatory fees, service fees, municipal charges, administration, then penalties
Quarterly due dates in the first 20 days of January or of each quarter
Garbage fees for businesses scaled by floor area, a simple base for a municipality starting a collection service
The rule that a company's officers answer for its violations and that a fine does not wipe out the unpaid tax
change: Reset every business tax schedule to the ceilings in BLGC s. 167, including the half rate for dealers in essential goods and the exclusion of duly registered Islamic banks

Rewrite the late-payment clause: BLGC s. 191 still caps the surcharge at 25% and interest at 2% a month for 36 months, but BLGC s. 153 lets the council replace interest with a Shari'ah-compliant late-payment rule, which most BARMM councils will want to consider
Raise the penal clause to the range in BLGC s. 576 (fines of ₱40,000 to ₱1,200,000 and 1 to 6 months in jail); the code's ₱1,000 floor falls below it
Hold the public hearings and publication that BLGC s. 212 and s. 213 require, and note that rates can then be adjusted only once every 5 years by up to 10% under BLGC s. 216
Drop the socialized housing tax and special levy unless the council will pass the enabling ordinances; the special levy must follow BLGC s. 266 (up to 60% of cost, 5 to 10 annual instalments)
barmm.fits: Municipalities writing their first full revenue code, especially fast-growing towns along the Cotabato–Marawi and Cotabato–Isulan roads.

ordinances.title: Amending several provisions of City Ordinance No. 8182, entitled "An ordinance providing for comprehensive welfare for the children of the City of Manila, and for other purposes", enacted on December 16, 2008 and approved on March 13, 2009, and inserting several provisions thereto…
ordinances.shortTitle: Manila City Children's Welfare Code of 2023
ordinances.summary: This is a full children's code in 13 articles. It replaces Manila's 2009 children's welfare ordinance and covers children's survival, development, participation and protection rights, plus children in need of special protection. It sets up the Manila Council for the Protection of Children with district and barangay councils, and it penalises establishments and parents for listed acts.
points: Creates the Manila Council for the Protection of Children (MCPC), District Councils (DCPC), Barangay Councils (BCPC) and a Manila BCPC Federation. The city funds the councils with at least 1% of its IRA, and each barangay gives its BCPC at least 1% of its budget.
Computer shops and internet cafes may not let children game from 8 pm to 7 am, or from 7 am to 5 pm on school days, and must post child-abuse reporting signs.
Parents and guardians are barred from corporal punishment, from refusing a child's healthcare or intervention programs, and from letting children loiter or sleep in public places from 10 pm to 4 am.
Bans selling firecrackers to minors, overloading tricycles or pedicabs used as school service, and discriminating against a child in admission, enrolment or services.
Requires lactation stations, a children's desk in every police station, child-friendly buildings and a children's rights hotline. November is declared Children's Month.
ordinances.penalties: Establishments: ₱1,000, then ₱3,000, then ₱5,000 with permit revocation and closure. Adults: community service of 16 to 40 hours, fines of ₱2,000 to ₱5,000 graded by the child's age, or up to 1 year in jail.
ordinances.amends: City Ordinance No. 8182 (2008), which it supersedes
ordinances.caveat: Section 118 on adult penalties has garbled cross-references (it cites Sections 120 and 121, which are the final clauses) and lists the age band of 15 to 17 years twice. It was approved by the Mayor on 1 June 2023.

barmm.why: Child malnutrition, child labour and displacement are persistent problems in BARMM, and the BLGC now requires councils for the protection of children down to the barangay. Manila's code is a full, recent model for those councils and for child protection rules. But several of its offences are written for a dense city, and some, like fining parents for corporal punishment, need careful handling before they are copied.
adopt: The council structure from city to barangay, with a federation of barangay councils and a fixed budget share for each
The rules for computer shops on gaming hours and child-abuse reporting signs, and graduated fines for establishments of ₱1,000, ₱3,000, then ₱5,000 with permit revocation
Bans on selling firecrackers to minors, overloading tricycles used as school service, and discriminating against children in admission or services
Lactation stations, a children's desk at police stations and a children's rights hotline
change: Re-cite the councils to BLGC s. 130 and s. 408, and replace '1% of the IRA' with the BLGC's own floor: at least 1% of the annual budget for the local council for the protection of children (BLGC s. 348)
Rename the Manila social welfare department as the social welfare and development officer, a licensed social worker under BLGC s. 537

Rewrite the curfew-type rule on children loitering from 10 pm to 4 am so that only parents face sanctions and children are referred to the social welfare office, in line with the national Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act (RA 9344, as amended) on status offences

Pair the corporal punishment ban with positive-discipline sessions run with the social welfare office and religious leaders, and use fines only for repeat cases; a fine-first approach is likely to be ignored and resented

Fix Section 118's garbled cross-references and duplicated age band, and cap penalties at ₱5,000 and 1 year for a city (BLGC s. 509), 6 months for a municipality (BLGC s. 489) and ₱3,000 for a barangay (BLGC s. 419)
barmm.fits: Cities and large municipalities such as Cotabato City, Marawi and Lamitan; the barangay council articles suit every barangay.

ordinances.title: Ordinance providing for a comprehensive children's code in the City of Bacolod
ordinances.shortTitle: Bacolod City Children's Code of 2015
ordinances.summary: A local children's code in 66 articles that sets out children's rights to survival, development, protection and participation, and the duties of parents, the community and city offices. It puts in place health, nutrition, education, child protection and participation programmes, and funds them through a dedicated Children's Fund.
points: Children's Fund of at least 1% of the IRA, separate from the 1% already required under the Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act
Local Council for the Protection of Children chaired by the Mayor, with a technical working group and the City Planning and Development Office as secretariat
Children's desks in all police stations; all government offices must adopt a child protection policy
The business permit office must start cancelling the permits of establishments using children in prostitution or lewd shows
Mandatory reporting of child abuse by heads of medical, school and other institutions; failure to report is punishable under RA 7610
Annual Children's Summit; implementing rules due within 90 days of approval

barmm.why: BARMM has some of the country's highest rates of child stunting, unregistered births and children out of school. Children there are also displaced by fighting and floods, in Marawi, the Liguasan Marsh towns and the SGA. A single children's code that ties together health, nutrition, education, protection and participation, with its own fund, gives a council one place to set duties. Several of Bacolod's references are now out of date or national-only, though.
adopt: The 4 rights framework (survival, development, protection, participation) and the duties it sets for parents, the community and LGU offices
Mandatory reporting of child abuse by heads of hospitals, schools and other institutions, with immunity for good-faith reporting
Children in emergencies: first priority in relief and family reunification, and child protection policies in every LGU office
Children's participation through children's groups and an annual summit, and implementing rules within 90 days
change: Replace 'IRA' with the National Tax Allotment and re-cite the fund to BLGC s. 348, which already requires at least 1% of the budget for the local council for the protection of children; decide honestly whether the LGU can afford a 2nd, separate 1% on top.
Re-cite the Local Council for the Protection of Children to BLGC s. 130, and add the barangay councils that BLGC s. 408 puts in every barangay.

Name the BARMM offices: the nutrition action officer (BLGC s. 548) with the Bangsamoro Nutrition Commission (BAA No. 83), and the social welfare officer (s. 537), who is the natural secretariat. Cover Madaris in the education, feeding and school board articles (BLGC s. 110 and s. 112, BAA No. 18).

Add articles Bacolod does not have: children in armed conflict under the national law RA 11188, displaced children under BAA No. 62, and child marriage under the national law RA 11596. Write that last one with Shari'ah court officials and ulama, not around them.
Make birth registration concrete, with mobile and late registration drives in island and upland barangays, because the Bacolod article is one line.
barmm.fits: Cities and provinces first, such as Cotabato City, Marawi and Lanao del Sur; municipalities can adopt a shorter version built around the LCPC and the barangay councils.

ordinances.title: The Child Welfare Code of Loon, amending for this purpose Municipal Ordinance No. 06-002, Series of 2006
ordinances.shortTitle: Child Welfare Code of Loon
ordinances.summary: A full child welfare code for Loon setting out children's rights and duties, the roles of families, schools, media, councils and businesses, and the town's programs for health, child development, emergencies and children in conflict with the law. It adds local prohibitions on top of national child protection laws and creates the town's child welfare councils and desks.
points: Prohibits children from betting in illegal numbers games and from being in gambling places
Video game shops and internet cafes serving children from 7:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. on school days or after 7:00 p.m. face a 15-day permit suspension, then 1 month, then confiscation and cancellation
Bars children 14 and below from using smartphones, tablets and computers except for authorised schooling or emergencies
Creates the Municipal Council for the Welfare of Children, Barangay Councils for the Protection of Children, a Desk for Children's Concerns and a Crisis Intervention Center
Sets a diversion system for child offenders at barangay and police level, including Katarungang Pambarangay conciliation
Hospital and clinic heads, teachers and government workers must report suspected child abuse
ordinances.penalties: Up to 6 months in jail and/or ₱2,500 per offence; a first-time parent, teacher or relative who admits the offence may get seminars, counselling or family therapy instead
ordinances.amends: Municipal Ordinance No. 06-002, Series of 2006 (The Child Welfare Code of Loon, Bohol)
ordinances.caveat: The Mayor's approval date is blank in this copy.

barmm.why: BARMM has high rates of child stunting, out-of-school children and child marriage, and children are still drawn into armed conflict and displacement. A single child welfare code gives a town one place to set out the councils, desks, reporting duties and diversion steps that national laws require. Loon's code is full but was written for a Catholic Visayan town, so parts need rework.
adopt: The Municipal Council for the Welfare of Children, Barangay Councils for the Protection of Children, a children's desk and a crisis intervention centre
The duty of hospital heads, teachers and government workers to report suspected child abuse
Diversion of child offenders at barangay and police level, and counselling instead of jail for a first-time parent or teacher who admits the offence
Bans on selling liquor, cigarettes and rugby to children and on arranging the marriage of children, which match the national ban on child marriage (RA 11596)
change: Re-cite the councils to BLGC s. 130 and s. 408 (the BCPC and child development centres), and fund the children's council with at least 1% of the budget under BLGC s. 348

Drop the ban on phones, tablets and computers for children 14 and below. It cannot be enforced, reaches into the home, and would cut off children who use phones for modular classes and madrasah lessons. Also drop confiscation of computer units, which goes beyond the fines BLGC s. 489 allows; use permit suspension

Check barangay diversion and conciliation against BLGC s. 427 and s. 436, and against the juvenile justice law (RA 9344 as amended, national law). Add a chapter on children in armed conflict under RA 11188 (national law) and on displaced children under BAA No. 62

Rewrite the school rules, on pregnancy and on enrolling children born outside marriage, to fit the Bangsamoro Education Code (BAA No. 18) and to cover madaris. Name mosques, ustadz and imams alongside churches

Tying a parenting course to the marriage licence will miss most marriages under Muslim law or custom, since many need no licence; run it through the Shari'ah circuit registrar, imams and the MSWDO instead
barmm.fits: Municipalities with active MSWDOs, especially conflict-affected and displacement-hit towns in Maguindanao del Sur, Maguindanao del Norte and Lanao del Sur.

ordinances.title: Enacting the revised 2022 La Union Investment and Incentives Code
ordinances.shortTitle: La Union Investment and Incentives Code of 2022
ordinances.summary: Sets the rules for attracting local and foreign investors to La Union through provincial tax breaks and other support. It creates an investment board and a one-stop promotion center, lists priority investment areas, and sets registration, reporting and sanction rules for registered enterprises. The tax incentives cover only the provincial share of taxes.
points: Creates the La Union Investment and Incentives Board (LUIIB) and the La Union Investment and Incentives Promotion Center (LUIIPC) as a one-stop processing center
Fiscal incentives: an extra 35% off the provincial share of basic real property tax and exemption from franchise, printing, amusement and annual fixed taxes, each for 1 year
Exemption from the Governor's permit and related business fees for 3 years, or at the Governor's discretion
Enterprises must apply within 6 months of getting their business permit; incentives may be availed only once and are non-transferable
Late reports are fined ₱3,000, ₱4,000 and ₱5,000, with cancellation of registration on the 4th infraction; appeals within 15 days
Sets an initial fund of ₱1,500,000 for the board and center
ordinances.penalties: ₱5,000 or up to 1 year in jail, or both; late reports ₱3,000 to ₱5,000, then cancellation of registration

barmm.why: BARMM provinces want investors for agriculture, fisheries, halal food processing and tourism, and an investment board with a one-stop center gives investors one door to knock on. The province's share of the tax is small, though, so the tax breaks will matter less to an investor than security, land titles and a fast permit. Build the code around the one-stop service and keep the incentives modest.
adopt: The investment and incentives board chaired by the governor, with sanggunian committee chairs and the league of municipalities on it
A one-stop promotion center that processes applications and keeps investors' records
The registration rules: apply within 6 months of the business permit, incentives used once and not transferable
Escalating fines for late reports, with cancellation of registration on the 4th infraction and a 15-day appeal
change: Fold the promotion center into the Business One-Stop Shop the BLGC already requires (s. 151) instead of running a second window, and staff it with the optional local economic and investment promotion officer
Have the provincial development council draft the investment priority areas and incentives, since BLGC s. 121 gives it that job

Make the incentives top up, not duplicate, the 6-year pioneer and 4-year non-pioneer exemptions for enterprises certified by the Bangsamoro Board of Investments (BLGC s. 156). Confirm in the full BLGC text that a sanggunian may grant tax exemptions by ordinance; that power is not in the summaries here
Cost the real property tax break against the province's 35% share under BLGC s. 297; the municipality's 40% and the barangay's 25% cannot be waived by the province
Keep the ₱5,000 or 1-year penalty (allowed for a province under BLGC s. 521), and scale the ₱1,500,000 start-up fund to the province's own income
barmm.fits: Provinces with growing farm and fishery investment, such as Maguindanao del Norte and Maguindanao del Sur; a city version works for Cotabato City.

ordinances.shortTitle: 2018 Investments and Incentives Code of the City of San Fernando
ordinances.summary: Sets San Fernando's investment policy and the local incentives it may grant to businesses that register. It creates an investments board and a one-stop investment centre, lists investment priority areas for 2018 to 2023, and sets the period of tax exemptions by enterprise size. Registered enterprises take on corporate social responsibility and environmental duties.
points: Creates the 19-member City of San Fernando Investments and Incentives Board (CSF-IIB) and the Investments Promotion and Assistance Center (CSF-IPAC) as a one-stop processing centre
Incentives apply only to activities on the Investment Priority Areas list for 2018 to 2023, which the board reviews periodically
Local tax exemption periods: large (above ₱100M) 6 years, medium (₱15M to ₱100M) 4 years, small (₱3M to ₱15M) 3 years, micro (below ₱3M) 2 years
Incentives never cover regulatory fees, service charges such as garbage and inspection fees, or utility charges; no double availment
5% of incentives availed must go to CSR projects; BOI pioneer-status enterprises are monitored from the 4th year
Refusing environmental compliance inspection is ground for forfeiting incentives and revoking registration or business permit
ordinances.amends: Repeals City Ordinance No. 2006-03 (Investment Incentive Code of the City of San Fernando)

Its legal basis, though, rests on RA 7160 and the national Board of Investments, both of which change in BARMM.
adopt: A short, periodically reviewed list of investment priority areas as the gate for any incentive
Exemption periods scaled by enterprise size, and the bar on double availment
The rule that incentives never cover regulatory fees, service charges or utility charges
The 5% CSR share and forfeiture of incentives for refusing environmental inspection

Find the BLGC provision that lets a sanggunian grant local tax exemptions before drafting; the code cites RA 7160 s. 192, and BLGC s. 218 withdraws most existing exemptions, so the basis must be confirmed with the MILG or the Ministry of Finance
Have the investment priorities come from the local development council under BLGC s. 121, and fold the one-stop investment centre into the Business One-Stop Shop required by BLGC s. 151
Shrink the 19-member board for smaller LGUs, and staff the centre with the local economic investment promotion officer BLGC s. 481 allows
Add priority areas BARMM actually has (halal processing, seaweed, marine products, Islamic finance), and require that large projects consult affected communities before approval under BLGC s. 32
barmm.fits: Cities (Cotabato City, Lamitan, Marawi) and growth-centre municipalities such as Parang, Bongao and Wao.

ordinances.title: Creating the Muntinlupa City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office and providing funds therefor
ordinances.shortTitle: Muntinlupa City DRRM Office ordinance
ordinances.summary: This ordinance creates the Muntinlupa City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (MCDRRMO) under the Office of the City Mayor, as RA 10121 requires. It lists the office's 26 functions, sets its staffing plan and sets up the city's DRRM fund.
points: The MCDRRMO is headed by a Department Head II with an Assistant Department Head II.

It has 3 divisions: Administrative and Training, Research and Planning, and Warning and Operation. Warning and Operation has a Rescue Operation Unit with medical, tactical and trauma sections, and a Warning and Communication Unit.

The Muntinlupa City DRRM Fund is at least 5% of estimated revenue from regular sources. 30% is a Quick Response Fund, and 70% goes to prevention, mitigation, preparedness, response, rehabilitation and recovery.
Staff salaries go into the 2014 Executive Budget and every year after, following CSC and DBM rules.
Posts are filled first from existing city employees, with new hires only if none are available.

barmm.why: Floods from the Rio Grande de Mindanao and the Liguasan Marsh, landslides in Lanao del Sur and storm surges in Tawi-Tawi and Basilan make a staffed DRRM office essential, and the BLGC lists a DRRM officer among the offices every province and municipality must have. The DRRM fund of at least 5% of estimated revenue from regular sources, split 30% quick response and 70% prevention to recovery
Filling posts first from existing employees, with new hires only if none are available
Charging salaries to the next executive budget and every year after

Yet some provincial DRRM offices exist only on paper or run on detailed staff. This short ordinance creates the office, lists its functions and sets a minimum staff of 4 in 6 pages. That is close to what a BARMM province needs.

The minimum staff of an officer plus 3 for administration and training, research and planning, and operations and warning, with degree and experience requirements
Funding through the DRRM fund, endorsed by the council to the sanggunian for appropriation
The duty to involve women, children, older persons and persons with disability in risk assessment and planning

Re-check the salary grades (SG-22 and SG-18) against the province's income class, and fill the posts under BLGC s. 87 and s. 91 and the Bangsamoro Civil Service Code (BAA No. 17).

Spell out that barangay development councils act as barangay DRRM councils under BLGC s. 121, and give the office a duty to support them.
barmm.fits: Provinces (Lanao del Sur, Maguindanao del Norte, Maguindanao del Sur, Basilan, Tawi-Tawi); cities and municipalities can use it with the officer post from BLGC s. 481.

At least 5% of estimated regular revenue goes to the LDRRMF, with at least 30% of that held as the Quick Response Fund

Bacoor's 2026 code is current. It uses the Incident Command System, anticipatory action under RA 12287 and damage assessment rules, which gives a BARMM LGU a modern frame to copy.
adopt: The Emergency Operations Center, Incident Command System and response clusters
Pre-disaster risk assessment leading to anticipatory action, early warning, and evacuation centre standards
The volunteer programme, youth DRRM groups in high schools and the role for amateur radio, which is useful where mobile signal is weak
Data privacy rules for victim and damage data under RA 10173, and named no-build zones

Treat displacement from armed conflict as a hazard, and link evacuation, camp management and return to BAA No. 62 (IDPs), the IDP council in BLGC s. 130 and the property tax exemption for displaced owners in BLGC s. 260
Keep jail terms within BLGC s. 489 for municipalities (₱5,000 or 6 months) and s. 509 for cities (₱5,000 or 1 year). Post the penal parts under BLGC s. 571, translated into the local language

ordinances.title: A comprehensive municipal code providing for the sustainable management, development and conservation of the municipal waters and its coastal resources, harmonizing and integrating all ordinances pertinent thereto and for other purposes
ordinances.shortTitle: Coastal Resource Management Code of Loon, Bohol
ordinances.summary: Loon's basic fisheries and coastal code. It brings the town's earlier fishery ordinances into one code under the Fisheries Code of 1998. It zones the municipal waters, governs licensing, marine sanctuaries, mangroves, fish corrals and aquaculture, and sets up the offices that enforce it. It applies to all fisherfolk, businesses and others who use the town's coastal and fishery resources.
points: Divides municipal waters into 6 zones: multiple use, rehabilitation, trade and navigation, tourism and recreation, protected (sanctuaries, no-take) and NIPAS

Closed season for danggit (siganid) during the 3rd to 5th rising of the new moon; catching, selling or possessing siganid fry is banned (₱1,000, ₱1,500, then ₱2,000 with confiscation, or 30 days in jail)
Bans trawl, compressor, lawag, electric shiner, liba-liba/hulbot-hulbot and beach seine fishing, sand extraction, mangrove conversion and anchoring in dive sites and sanctuaries
Fisherfolk registered in other towns pay double the license rate; marginal fisherfolk pay no other fee for the municipal fishery license
Creates a CRM Section under the Municipal Agriculturist, a Municipal FARMC and a Municipal Bantay Dagat Council
50% of fines collected go as cash incentives to the team that made the arrest and those who helped
ordinances.penalties: General penalty ₱1,000 to ₱2,500, or 1 to 6 months in jail, or both; specific gear bans carry ₱2,000 to ₱2,500 and up to 1 year, with boats and gear forfeited
ordinances.amends: Harmonizes and integrates earlier Loon fishery ordinances (e.g. MO 1981-1, MO 1992-02, MO 1994-1, MO 1994-03, MO 1995-4) and repeals inconsistent ordinances

barmm.why: Coastal and lake towns in BARMM depend on municipal waters but often have only scattered fishery ordinances. Loon's code puts zoning, licensing, sanctuaries, mangroves, banned gear and a Bantay Dagat in one place. That suits island towns in Tawi-Tawi and Basilan, the Moro Gulf coast of the Maguindanao provinces and Lanao del Sur, and the Lake Lanao towns, where seaweed farms, fish corrals and dynamite or compressor fishing all compete for the same water.
adopt: The zoning of municipal waters into multiple use, rehabilitation, navigation, tourism and protected no-take zones
The gear bans (trawl, compressor, electric shiner, beach seine and similar), the ban on mangrove conversion and the ban on anchoring in sanctuaries
A CRM section under the municipal agriculturist, a municipal FARMC and a Bantay Dagat council
Double license rates for fishers registered in other towns, and the 50% share of fines for the arresting team
change: Re-cite the basis to BLGC s. 172 and s. 480 (exclusive municipal authority over fishery privileges and enforcement of fishery laws in municipal waters) and to national law, RA 8550 as amended by RA 10654; Loon's code predates the 2015 amendments and their higher penalties
Cap every jail term at 6 months and every fine at ₱5,000 (BLGC s. 489). Several of Loon's clauses run to 1 year or say only 'not less than 6 months', which a municipality cannot impose

Make sure marginal fishers using nets, traps and traditional gear such as payao pay no charge, and give their organizations first right to fish corrals and aquatic beds, as BLGC s. 172 requires. Check the siganid fry ban against that free fry-gathering right before copying it
Replace the species and closed seasons with local ones, and add rules for seaweed farm plots in Tawi-Tawi or freshwater cages in Lake Lanao
Put the CRM section under the agriculturist and coordinate mangrove work with the environment officer (BLGC s. 536 and s. 538)

ordinances.title: Clean lifestyle ordinance prohibiting the use of e-cigarettes in certain places, imposing penalties for violations thereof and providing funds therefor
ordinances.shortTitle: Clean Lifestyle and Smoke-Free Bacolod Ordinance
ordinances.summary: Bans vaping in enclosed and public places, workplaces and public vehicles outside approved vaping areas, and restricts the sale, advertising and promotion of tobacco products and e-cigarettes in Bacolod City. It sets up a task force, a citation ticket system and a smoking cessation programme, with a yearly budget.
points: Bans selling tobacco or vapes to minors, within 100 metres of schools, playgrounds and health facilities, by street vendors, or without a permit
Bans tobacco and vape advertising where minors are allowed, open shelf display, and government officials' partnerships with the tobacco industry
Clean Lifestyle and Smoke-Free Task Force chaired by the Mayor, with the health and environment committee chairs as co-chairs
Citation tickets payable at the City Treasurer within 5 business days; a no-contest payment is allowed for 1st and 2nd offences; community service is allowed for those who cannot pay
At least ₱1,000,000 a year goes into a trust fund; 10% of each fine goes to the apprehending officer
Permits are suspended for 1 week to 1 month, or revoked, if violations are not fixed within 15 days
ordinances.penalties: ₱2,000 for a 1st offence, ₱5,000 for a 2nd, ₱10,000 and/or up to 3 months in jail for a 3rd, plus permit suspension or revocation for businesses

barmm.why: Smoking and vaping are common among young men in BARMM's towns and cities, and many Muslim scholars already discourage both, so a local smoke- and vape-free rule has social backing. This ordinance gives a working enforcement model: banned places, sales near schools, a task force, citation tickets and a cessation program. Its fines and fine-sharing need rework, and parts of it now overlap with the national vape law passed in 2022.

Bans on sales to minors, by street vendors and without a permit, and on open shelf display and advertising where minors are allowed

Check the vape rules against RA 9211 and RA 11900, the national vape law, which sets its own age limit and sales rules; local rules must not contradict it
Chair the task force through the local health board in BLGC s. 114 with the health officer, and keep the yearly fund as a trust fund only if used strictly for its purpose under BLGC s. 333
Post the ordinance for 6 weeks, publish it and translate it into local languages as BLGC s. 571 requires for penal ordinances
barmm.fits: Cities (Cotabato City, Marawi, Lamitan) and large municipalities with schools and markets in the centre, such as Parang, Datu Odin Sinsuat and Bongao.

ordinances.shortTitle: Smoke Free Ordinance of the Province of Bataan
ordinances.summary: Bans smoking in enclosed and partly enclosed public places, workplaces and public vehicles across Bataan, and restricts tobacco sales and advertising. It sets graduated fines, a citation ticket system, a smoking cessation program and a Smokefree Task Force chaired by the Governor. It applies to all persons and places in the province.
points: Bans tobacco sales to minors and within 100 meters of schools, playgrounds, hospitals and health offices
Bans cinema and outdoor tobacco ads and ad materials outside point-of-sale premises
Licences of establishments or vehicles can be suspended for 1 week to 1 month if a violation is not fixed within 15 days or a citation is unpaid within 7 working days
Violators who cannot pay may do community service, each hour reducing the fine by 3 times the hourly minimum wage
Allocates ₱500,000 at the start and at least ₱500,000 a year; fines go to a trust fund for the task force
Establishments are inspected starting 90 days after the ordinance takes effect
ordinances.penalties: ₱500 to ₱5,000 depending on the act and offence; a 3rd offence can bring up to 1 year in jail and suspension or revocation of the business permit

barmm.why: Smoking is widespread among men in BARMM, and few LGUs here have a smoke-free ordinance with real enforcement. Bataan's ordinance is a complete model: bans, a citation ticket, a cessation program, a funded task force and a rule keeping the tobacco industry off it. It needs updating for vapes and for who in BARMM issues business permits.
adopt: The ban on tobacco sales to minors and within 100 metres of schools, playgrounds, hospitals and health offices
The citation ticket system, the 15-day and 7-working-day deadlines before suspension, and community service for violators who cannot pay
A smokefree task force that excludes anyone tied to the tobacco industry, with deputised civilian enforcers
A yearly budget of at least ₱500,000 and fines kept in a trust fund for the task force, which BLGC s. 333 allows

ordinances.shortTitle: Smoking ban in public places
ordinances.summary: Bans smoking in a list of public places in Naga City, including entertainment venues, government offices, shops and markets, public vehicles, schools, hospitals and places of worship. Owners, managers and drivers who allow smoking are liable along with smokers. Government offices must provide ventilated smoking areas; private businesses may choose to.
points: Covers bars, restaurants, cockpits, theatres, libraries, government offices, stores and markets, elevators, buses, jeepneys and trimobiles, classrooms, hospitals, clinics, churches and mosques
Bans smoking in warehouses for flammable materials and within 50 metres of them or of carriers of such materials
No smoking areas allowed in schools, public vehicles or fuel and explosives storage; where allowed, they must be well ventilated and are monitored by the city engineer

Smokers: ₱200, ₱300, ₱500, then ₱1,000 and prosecution

Explicit coverage of mosques, schools, hospitals and public transport

ordinances.summary: A 23-chapter code that gathers Bacoor's rules on public health, sanitation and safety into one document. Health certificate applicants need fecalysis, sputum test or chest X-ray and a drug test; lab results are valid 30 days, X-ray and drug test 6 months
Sets up the City Epidemiological and Testing Unit and the City Social Hygiene Clinic
Separate sub-codes for markets (with a Bacoor City Market Board), the city slaughterhouse, water, motels, pools, cemeteries and nuisance abatement
A food establishment that lets a sick person handle food pays ₱5,000 and loses its sanitary permit

Cholera, diarrhoea and other waterborne diseases still break out after floods. Bacoor's code turns PD 856 into local chapters with permits, fees and graded penalties, but it is long and written for a suburban city.
adopt: The health certificate system for food handlers, water refilling stations, salons, clinics and funeral parlours
The chapters on food establishments, markets, water supply, public toilets, sewage and nuisance abatement
Graded penalties for a 1st, 2nd and 3rd offence, with sanitary permit suspension and cancellation
Letting the mayor's committees write implementing guidelines for each chapter

Check that per-day fines cannot add up past ₱5,000, the cap in BLGC s. 489 and s. 509, and post the code as a penal ordinance under BLGC s. 571
barmm.fits: Cities and larger municipalities with a licensed health officer and sanitary inspectors, such as Cotabato City, Marawi, Lamitan and Bongao.

The certificate is valid to the end of the year and renewed every year.
No food establishment may open without a sanitary permit posted in a conspicuous place. A new occupant must report a change of ownership within 14 days.

There are 25 chapters covering food establishments, schools, water supply, markets, hotels and boarding houses, ports and airports, vermin, laundries, swimming pools, cemeteries, sewage, solid waste, livestock farms, barber and beauty shops, night clubs, spas, caterers and ambulant vendors, and nuisances.
No provincial, city or municipal employee may deal directly with an establishment to facilitate a sanitary permit or health certificate.
Anyone who obstructs health officers or defaces posted notices faces up to 1 year in jail or a fine of not less than ₱5,000, or both.
ordinances.penalties: Establishments: ₱2,500, then ₱5,000, then closure and revocation of permit. Individuals: ₱1,000 and/or up to 5 days in jail, rising to ₱5,000 and/or up to 30 days for a 3rd offence.
ordinances.caveat: The OCR is garbled in places, and the governor's approval block cannot be read.

barmm.why: Food-borne and water-borne illness is a steady problem in BARMM markets, carinderias, boarding houses and evacuation sites, and few LGUs have one sanitation code that inspectors can enforce. Pangasinan's code turns PD 856, a national law that still applies, into local permit and health certificate rules across 25 kinds of establishments. The structure carries over well, but the offices, penalty wording and some chapters need rework, and the garbled OCR means the text should be redrafted, not pasted.
adopt: Health certificates for food handlers and other covered workers, renewed every year after basic tests
No food establishment opens without a sanitary permit posted in view, and changes of ownership reported within 14 days
The ban on any LGU employee acting as a fixer for permits or certificates
The chapter-by-chapter standards for markets, water supply, schools, boarding houses, ports, cemeteries and ambulant vendors
change: Name the provincial health officer as lead enforcer under BLGC s. 532, have the health board review the code and its budget (BLGC s. 114), and coordinate with the Ministry of Health (BLGC s. 117)
Fix the obstruction penalty: 'not less than ₱5,000' sets a floor, but BLGC s. 521 caps provincial fines at ₱5,000 and jail at 1 year. A municipal version must cap jail at 6 months (BLGC s. 489)
Drop or rewrite chapters that do not fit local rules, such as night clubs where the LGU bans them, and add halal handling and slaughterhouse sanitation, which municipalities run under BLGC s. 480
Add sanitation for evacuation centres and water points for displaced families, in line with BAA No. 62 on internally displaced persons
Post the penal ordinance for 6 weeks and translate it into local languages before it takes effect (BLGC s. 571)
barmm.fits: Provinces with a working provincial health office, and cities such as Cotabato City and Marawi.

ordinances.title: The Transportation and Traffic Code of the Municipality of Loon, Bohol
ordinances.shortTitle: Transportation and Traffic Code of the Municipality of Loon, Bohol
ordinances.summary: A full municipal traffic code covering every vehicle on public or private roads in Loon. It sets traffic rules, creates the bodies that manage and enforce them, regulates tricycle franchises and habal-habal motorcycles-for-hire, runs the transport terminal and cruise ship port traffic, and lists local fines for each violation.
points: Creates a Municipal Franchising and Regulatory Board, a Municipal Traffic Management Board, a Municipal Traffic Management Office under the Mayor, and Municipal Traffic Aides (MUTRA).
Requires helmets for motorcycle drivers and back-riders on every road, bans improvised mufflers, and sets speed limits, overtaking, right-of-way, parking and impounding rules.

Designates the Loon Bus Terminal at Mercado de Loon with daily parking fees, such as ₱10 for buses and jeepneys, ₱4 for tricycles and habal-habal, and ₱50 for 10-wheeler trucks; overnight parking is double.
Habal-habal operators pay a ₱300 Mayor's permit fee with sticker and ID, and drivers must wear an ID, shoes and a long-sleeve uniform.
At the Loon International Cruise Ship Port: 2 police outposts on 24-hour duty, vehicle users' charges from ₱2 to ₱350 a day, and a ₱2 environmental fee per passenger.
Violators have 7 days to pay a citation ticket before a court case is filed; fines are shared 75% to the general fund and 25% to MTMO and MUTRA operations.
ordinances.penalties: A schedule of local fines by offence, for example ₱500, ₱1,000 and ₱1,500 for driving without a valid licence, capped at ₱2,500; the general penalty is ₱300, ₱500 and ₱1,000 for the 1st, 2nd and 3rd offences.
ordinances.amends: Repeals any inconsistent provision of previous ordinances; it carries over sections of Municipal Ordinance 1996-08 on tricycle franchising.

barmm.why: BARMM towns run on tricycles, habal-habal and jeepneys, with few traffic offices and fewer written rules, and helmetless motorcycle crashes are a leading cause of injury on the highways through Maguindanao and Lanao del Sur. This is a full municipal code with boards, aides, a terminal, tricycle franchising, habal-habal permits and a fine schedule. Strip out the cruise port parts and fit the bodies to a small town's payroll.
adopt: Helmet rules for drivers and back-riders, the ban on improvised mufflers, and the speed, overtaking, right-of-way and parking rules
Habal-habal permits with sticker and ID, and driver ID and uniform rules
A municipal terminal with posted daily parking fees, double for overnight
Citation tickets with 7 days to pay before a case is filed, and a fine schedule capped well under the legal limit
change: Re-cite tricycle franchising to BLGC s. 480 and keep fees within BLGC s. 156, which bars LGUs from taxing common carriers or charging motor vehicle registration fees except for tricycles
Keep every fine within ₱5,000 or 6 months under BLGC s. 489, and post and publish the code as BLGC s. 571 requires
Leave police deployment to national law and the Bangsamoro Organic Law (BLGC s. 33); the code should create civilian traffic aides, not order police posts
Drop the cruise ship port chapter; replace it with rules for the town's own market, ferry landing or pumpboat port where there is one
Merge the 3 bodies into 1 traffic and franchising board for 4th to 6th class municipalities; check the 25% fine share to MTMO against BLGC s. 329, since earmarked fines still need an appropriation
barmm.fits: Municipal centres on national highways, such as Parang, Datu Odin Sinsuat, Buluan, Wao, Malabang and Lamitan.
