ordinances.title: Adopting the 2015 Traffic Management Code of Marikina City
ordinances.shortTitle: The 2015 Traffic Management Code of Marikina City
ordinances.summary: This is a citywide traffic code covering all national and local roads in Marikina. It sets rules on signs and signals, general driving, giving way, speed, one-way streets, turns, stopping and parking, parking zones and fees, reckless driving and accidents. It is administered by the City Transportation Management and Development Office (CTMDO).
points: Motor vehicles may not drive or park on bicycle lanes or on the jogging lanes along the Marikina River.

Overnight parking is allowed only on listed streets. It costs ₱10 a night, collected by the barangay, or ₱750 a quarter or ₱1,500 a year paid to the City Treasurer. It is barred on roads under 3 metres wide and for buses, jeepneys, tricycles and trucks of 8 or more wheels.

Delivery vehicles entering the Marikina Public Market Zone pay ₱100 per entry for 6- to 10-wheelers, ₱50 for elf vans and ₱30 for jeepneys. Parking costs ₱10 for the first 2 hours and ₱20 per hour after, or ₱5 and ₱10 for motorcycles.
The Traffic Management and Enforcement Division may tow illegally parked vehicles at the owner's cost.
Repair shops must report to police within 24 hours any vehicle showing signs of an accident, crime or bullet strike, or face up to ₱5,000.
ordinances.caveat: The text covers only pages 1 to 19 of 42 and ends at Section 76, so the penalty schedule, the later articles, the enactment date and the signatures are missing.

barmm.verdict: Take the idea, not the text
barmm.why: Cotabato City, Marawi and fast-growing poblaciones like Parang and Bongao face traffic jams, tricycle crowding and parking at the market with few written rules. Marikina's code is a good outline for a citywide traffic code. But the text stops at Section 76, so it has no penalty schedule, enactment date or signatures, and some of its fees would be risky in BARMM.
adopt: The structure: signs and signals, right of way, speed, one-way streets, turns, stopping and parking, parking zones, reckless driving and accidents
Protected bicycle lanes and pedestrian paths that motor vehicles may not use or park on
Towing illegally parked vehicles at the owner's cost, and overnight parking only on listed streets and never on roads under 3 metres wide
Requiring repair shops to report to police within 24 hours any vehicle showing signs of an accident, crime or bullet strike
change: Write your own penalty schedule, since the text has none, within ₱5,000 and 1 year for a city (BLGC s. 509) or ₱5,000 and 6 months for a municipality (BLGC s. 489), and post and publish it as a penal ordinance under BLGC s. 571
Drop or rework the per-entry fees on delivery vehicles: BLGC s. 156 bars local taxes on goods passing through and on common carriers, so a fee must be tied to a real service such as market parking
Add tricycle franchising and routes, which municipalities control under BLGC s. 480, and keep national roads and driver rules under the national Land Transportation and Traffic Code (RA 4136)
Use BLGC s. 24 for street closures for markets, fiestas and Friday prayers, and set parking fees by ordinance under BLGC s. 148
barmm.fits: Cities and busy municipal centres: Cotabato City, Marawi, Lamitan, Parang, Datu Odin Sinsuat and Bongao.

ordinances.title: Ordinance enacting a market code of the Municipality of Trinidad, Bohol
ordinances.shortTitle: Trinidad Market Code of 2007
ordinances.summary: A market code for the Trinidad Public Market covering its board, stall bidding and leases, vendor rules, rents and fees, weights and measures, and slaughterhouse fees. It is a compact model for a town public market.
points: Trinidad Public Market Board chaired by the Mayor, which runs stall bidding and sets rates subject to council approval; a Market Administrator runs the market day to day
Occupancy privilege fees of ₱4,000 to ₱10,000 for wet-market stalls and ₱30,000 in the main building, plus rent of ₱4 per sq m a day
Stalls idle for 3 months (90 days) are declared vacant and rebid
Bans selling outside assigned sections, short weighing, living in stalls, subleasing stalls and videoke machines
Transient vendors pay ₱300 for a Mayor's permit; porters register for ₱50 a year; entrance fees of ₱0.10 to ₱1.00 per kilo
Late payment: 25% surcharge and 2% monthly interest for up to 36 months; 20% discount for payment in the first 5 days of the month
ordinances.penalties: ₱1,000 for a 1st violation, ₱1,500 for a 2nd, ₱2,000 plus revocation of permit and termination of lease for a 3rd
ordinances.caveat: This copy, posted by WIEGO, has no ordinance number, enactment date or signatures; the year comes from its short title.

barmm.why: The public market is often a BARMM town's largest own-source income, and many are run without a written code, so stall awards, arrears and subleasing turn into disputes. Trinidad's code is a compact model for a small town market, from the board to bidding, rents and meat inspection. The copy is unsigned and undated, and its money rules need BARMM-specific changes.
adopt: A market board chaired by the mayor, with a vendors' association seat, plus a market administrator for daily operations
Sealed public bidding for stalls, priority for local bidders, a standard lease and certificate of award, and rebidding of stalls idle for 90 days
Bans on short weighing, subleasing, living in stalls and selling outside assigned sections
Graduated penalties of ₱1,000, ₱1,500 and ₱2,000 with lease termination on the 3rd offence, which fit within BLGC s. 489
change: Trinidad's 25% surcharge and 2% monthly interest for 36 months are the maximum BLGC s. 191 allows; BLGC s. 153 lets the council use a Shari'ah-compliant fixed late charge instead, which most BARMM vendors will see as fairer. Keep the 20% early-payment discount.

Separate halal and non-halal meat: their own sections, stalls, tools and drainage, and pork kept away from the main meat line. Have meat inspection and slaughterhouse rules under the veterinarian (BLGC s. 543, optional for municipalities, so name who inspects).

Check the per-kilo entrance fees against BLGC s. 156, which bars taxing products sold by marginal farmers and fishers; exempt them or set a flat facility fee. Keep the transient vendor permit fee tied to regulation cost, since s. 167 caps the business tax on peddlers at ₱50 a year.
Run bidding through the Bids and Awards Committee under BLGC s. 387, hold public hearings on the rates (s. 212) and publish them (s. 213), and never let a private person collect market fees (s. 152).
Fill in the number, date and signatures yourself and re-price every fee; the 2007 Bohol rates are not a basis for a BARMM market.
barmm.fits: Municipalities with one public market and a slaughterhouse, such as town centres in Maguindanao del Sur, Lanao del Sur and the SGA.

ordinances.title: Ordinance requiring businesses and establishments in Davao City which offer halal products and services to acquire halal certification from the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF) accredited certifying bodies, prior to the posting of the word "halal" within their premises or to use the "halal" logo in their business name
ordinances.shortTitle: Halal Ordinance of Davao City
ordinances.summary: Requires any business in Davao City that sells or serves halal food or non-food products to be certified by an NCMF-accredited halal certifying body before it uses the word or logo "halal". It covers hotels, restaurants, eateries, food stalls, school canteens, function halls and producers, manufacturers and suppliers.
points: Covers halal food served at any event in the city, including seminars, weddings and birthdays
Certified establishments must display the Philippine Halal logo at the front and keep their certification documents on the premises
Displaying the halal word or logo without certification from an NCMF-accredited body is prohibited
A 3rd offence can bring revocation of the business permit and closure, at the court's discretion
ordinances.penalties: ₱500 to ₱1,000 for a 1st offence, ₱1,000 to ₱2,000 for a 2nd, ₱2,000 to ₱5,000 plus permit revocation and closure for a 3rd
ordinances.caveat: The text is noisy OCR; it was deemed approved after the Mayor let 10 days lapse under Section 54 of the Local Government Code.

barmm.why: A halal sign on a shop or a packaged product is a religious assurance, and in Cotabato City, Marawi and the regional centre at Parang false labels hurt both buyers and honest sellers. The ordinance is short and easy to enforce. But in a Muslim-majority region almost every eatery treats its food as halal, so a rule that punishes the word without certification could hit small carinderias first.
adopt: The ban on using the word or logo 'halal' without certification from an accredited certifying body
The duty to display the logo at the entrance and keep the certificate on the premises
Graded fines of ₱500 to ₱5,000 with permit revocation only on a 3rd offence, which fit within BLGC s. 489 and s. 509
change: Re-cite the legal basis to BLGC s. 17 (general welfare, including preserving culture) and the permit powers in BLGC s. 151, in place of the Local Government Code

The 2015 text names only the NCMF under RA 9997. Check the 2016 national halal law (RA 10817) for who now accredits certifiers. Also check the Bangsamoro Administrative Code (BAA No. 13) and current regional rules for any role of a Bangsamoro body such as the Darul-Ifta
Narrow the coverage to processed and packaged goods, hotels, caterers and chain outlets, and drop the clause on food at private weddings and birthdays, which in BARMM would reach every family kanduli
Add a grace period and a certification drive with the certifying bodies before any fines start, so small food sellers are not penalised for the cost of certification
Post and publish it as a penal ordinance under BLGC s. 571, in the local language
barmm.fits: Cities and trading towns with processors, hotels and food chains, such as Cotabato City, Marawi, Lamitan, Bongao and Parang.

ordinances.shortTitle: Halal Ordinance
ordinances.summary: Food businesses in Davao City that serve halal food must get halal accreditation from the Davao City Muslim Ulama Halal Certifying and Monitoring Agency before they display the word "halal" or use the halal logo. It covers restaurants, fast-food chains, eateries, cinema food stalls, school canteens and halal food served at events in function halls. The stated aim is to protect Muslims' right to religiously sanctioned food.
points: Covers restaurants, fast-food chains, eateries, moviehouse food stalls, school and university canteens, and halal food served at seminars, weddings and other events in function halls
Establishments must get accreditation, display the halal logo in front and display their accreditation documents on the premises
Halal food must not be prepared with kitchenware or utensils used for haram food
Bans mixing pork or other haram meat with meat used in halal-processed food
Defines halal-processed meat, haram meat and the certifying agency
ordinances.penalties: ₱500 to ₱1,000 for a 1st offence, ₱1,000 to ₱2,000 for a 2nd, and ₱2,000 to ₱5,000 with permit revocation and closure for a 3rd
ordinances.caveat: The approval stamp indicates the ordinance took effect by lapse without the mayor's signature under Section 54 of RA 7160; the scan's OCR is rough in places.

barmm.why: In most of BARMM, food is assumed to be halal, so the real risk is a 'halal' sign on food that is not, especially in mixed communities, school canteens, catered events and shops selling outside products. Davao's short ordinance ties the right to use the word 'halal' to accreditation and bans shared utensils and mixed meat. That fits Cotabato City, Lamitan, the SGA towns and other places with non-Muslim-owned eateries. It is less needed in Marawi or interior Lanao del Sur towns, where almost every eatery is Muslim-run.
adopt: No food business may display the word 'halal' or the halal logo without accreditation, and the documents must be posted on the premises
The ban on preparing halal food with kitchenware used for haram food, and on mixing haram meat into halal dishes
Coverage of school canteens and food served at seminars, weddings and other events in function halls
The 3-step fines from ₱500 up to ₱5,000 with permit revocation on the 3rd offence, which sit within BLGC caps
change: Don't name a single certifier in the ordinance. Recognize bodies accredited under national law (RA 10817), and check whether the Bangsamoro Government has issued halal rules; no halal BAA appears in the index
Widen the haram definition with local religious authorities: Davao's covers only pork and improperly killed animals and leaves out alcohol, blood and other ingredients

Re-cite the basis to the general welfare clause (BLGC s. 17, which covers preserving culture and public morals) and check halal status at business permit issuance through the Business One-Stop Shop (BLGC s. 151)
Keep fines within ₱5,000 (BLGC s. 509 for cities, s. 489 for municipalities), and replace the effectivity clause with the 6-week posting and translation rule in BLGC s. 571
barmm.fits: Cities and mixed-population municipalities such as Cotabato City, Lamitan and the SGA towns, and tourist towns with outside-owned eateries.

ordinances.title: Recognizing the right of Muslim women to wear hijab, niqab, or burqa in school campuses, workplaces, commercial establishments and other private or public premises and prohibiting unlawful discrimination and unreasonable restriction thereof and providing penalties thereto
ordinances.shortTitle: The Hijab Ordinance of Davao City
ordinances.summary: Protects the right of Muslim women in Davao City to wear the hijab, niqab or burqa in schools, workplaces, shops and other public or private premises. It bans refusing them entry, discouraging students from wearing them, or making their removal a condition of work. Institutions may still apply reasonable security checks, such as screening by a female guard.
points: Unlawful to refuse entry to a woman because she wears a hijab, niqab or burqa
Unlawful to discourage a female student from wearing one in class or in school activities such as contests and sports
Unlawful to bar it at work or make it a condition of work or ground for termination
Wearers must cooperate with reasonable security checks, such as screening by a female officer or uncovering for facial recognition
The Barangay Cultural Communities Affairs and Development office under the Mayor takes complaints and mediates, preferably within 7 working days
ordinances.penalties: Reprimand for a 1st offence, ₱1,000 for a 2nd, and ₱3,000 and/or 20 days in jail for a 3rd

barmm.why: Even in a mostly Muslim region, women are still told to remove the hijab or niqab in some private and church-run schools, hospitals, banks and malls, especially in Cotabato City, Lamitan and the mixed towns of the SGA and Maguindanao. The ordinance is short, clear and balanced, with a security-check proviso that answers the usual objection. It also shows how to protect a religious practice without punishing a first mistake.
adopt: The 3 prohibited acts: refusing entry, discouraging students, and making removal a condition of work
The security proviso allowing screening by a female officer or brief uncovering for identification
Definitions of hijab, niqab, burqa, institution and premises
Mediation of complaints within 7 working days before any case is filed
change: Re-cite the enacting clause to BLGC s. 17 and s. 509 (or s. 489 for a municipality); the fines are already within both limits

Give the complaint and mediation role to an office that exists in BARMM, such as the human rights action center in BLGC s. 480 or the legal officer in BLGC s. 535, with referral to the Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission (BAA No. 4)
Do not route complaints through the lupon: most respondents are schools and companies, and BLGC s. 436 excludes complaints against juridical entities from barangay settlement
Widen protection to the religious and cultural dress of Christian and Indigenous residents too (BAA No. 64); a one-sided rule is harder to defend and less fair in mixed communities
Replace the effectivity clause with the 6-week posting, publication and translation BLGC s. 571 requires, and make the 1st-offence reprimand a written warning rather than a criminal penalty
barmm.fits: Cities and mixed municipalities with private schools, hospitals and malls: Cotabato City, Lamitan, the SGA municipalities, Upi and South Upi.

ordinances.title: Ordinance providing for a Women's Development Code of Davao City and for other purposes
ordinances.shortTitle: Women Development Code of Davao City
ordinances.summary: An early, wide-ranging women's code that defines women's rights and violence against women, and sets city duties on health, education, work, culture, rural, Indigenous and Moro women, and gender and development. A second book sets penalties for trafficking, sex tours, forced marriage and labour violations, and creates an Integrated Gender and Development Office to implement it.
points: Creates the Integrated Gender and Development Office as the city's coordinating, regulatory and monitoring body for the code
Sets aside 6% of the Annual Development Fund, plus official development assistance under RA 7192
Creates a Council for Women, a city Women's Summit, a Women Complaints Relation Section and women's representation in barangay and city development councils
Provides for the rights of Indigenous and Moro women, including culturally appropriate schools
Bans soliciting women's services for sexual purposes, sex tours and forced marriage; establishments offering sex tours lose their business permit
City departments must report on compliance every 6 months
ordinances.penalties: Mostly a ₱5,000 fine and/or up to 1 year in jail; some labour and health provisions set fines of ₱1,000 to ₱5,000 or permit cancellation
ordinances.caveat: The text is OCR of the session minutes (Resolution No. 12878), which record floor amendments; some figures are hard to read.

barmm.verdict: Take the idea, not the text
barmm.why: Davao City's 1997 code is one of the few local women's codes with articles written for Moro and Indigenous women, including culturally appropriate schooling and access to schools and jobs for women whose births and marriages were never registered. That is directly useful for BARMM's mixed Moro, Teduray, Lambangian and settler communities. But the text is OCR of session minutes, its budget and penalty rules predate national laws now in force, and some clauses reach beyond what an LGU can do.
adopt: The articles on Moro and Indigenous women, including culturally appropriate schools and access to schools and jobs without birth or marriage certificates
A council for women, a yearly women's summit and a complaints desk
Women's seats in barangay and city development councils, which BLGC s. 119 now backs with a 40% target
Reports from every department on compliance every 6 months
change: Replace the 6% of the Annual Development Fund with at least 5% of the annual budget under BLGC s. 348, and add the sanctions in BLGC s. 582 and s. 584
Replace the Integrated Gender and Development Office with the Local Women's Development Officer (BLGC s. 547) under Bangsamoro Women Commission guidelines (BAA No. 8)
Drop the local penalties for trafficking and sex tours; national anti-trafficking law now covers them with much heavier penalties

Redraft the forced marriage clause with care: Muslim marriages fall under the Code of Muslim Personal Laws and the Shari'ah courts, and child marriage is now banned by national law (RA 11596); an LGU clause should focus on referral and protection, not new offences
Drop the sanctions on soldiers and police at checkpoints; under BLGC s. 33 control over the police is set by national law, so refer such cases to the proper bodies instead
barmm.fits: Municipalities and cities with mixed Moro, Indigenous and settler populations: the SGA, Upi and South Upi, and Cotabato City.

ordinances.title: Establishing Violence Against Women (VAW) Desk and protocol in handling VAW cases at the barangay level
ordinances.shortTitle: An Ordinance Establishing Violence Against Women (VAW) Desk and Protocol in Handling VAW Cases at the Barangay Level
ordinances.summary: This ordinance requires a Violence Against Women desk in every barangay of Davao City and sets a step-by-step protocol for barangay officials handling VAW cases. That protocol covers walk-in victims, cases reported by neighbours, protection orders and referrals.
points: Each punong barangay sets up a VAW desk in the barangay hall with furniture, a separate filing cabinet and logbooks. The desk person is trained in gender-sensitive case handling, preferably a woman kagawad or tanod.
The desk officer is on duty from 7 am to 7 pm, reachable by landline and mobile, and on call after hours.
Incidents must be reported to the PNP and the City Social Services and Development Office within 4 hours.

Victims are helped to file for a court TPO or PPO within 24 hours after a 15-day Barangay Protection Order is issued. Rape and trafficking cases go to the PNP Women and Children Protection Center or the NBI.
Funding comes from the GAD allocation of 5% of the annual barangay budget. Barangays file quarterly case reports with the City Mayor's Office through the Integrated Gender and Development Division.

barmm.why: In BARMM, many women who suffer violence go first to the barangay, and family or clan pressure pushes those cases toward settlement. The BLGC already requires a VAW desk in every barangay, but it does not say how the desk should handle a case. This short protocol fills that gap step by step and costs little to run.
adopt: The step-by-step protocol for walk-in victims and for cases reported by neighbours: safety and medical needs first, then rights, the intake sheet and the Barangay Protection Order
A trained desk officer, preferably a woman kagawad or tanod, with confidential records and a separate filing cabinet
Help to file for a court protection order within 24 hours of a BPO, and referral of rape and trafficking to the police women and children desk or the NBI
Quarterly case reports to the city or municipality
change: Re-cite the desk to BLGC s. 408 and the city's or municipality's role to its supervision over barangays (s. 37); RA 9262 and the Magna Carta of Women stay as the national law basis.
Add a plain rule that VAW cases are never brought to the lupon, mediation or settlement; BLGC s. 436 excludes them from amicable settlement. Say the same for settlement by elders or clan leaders.

Fund it from the 5% GAD budget in BLGC s. 348. Route reports to the social welfare officer (s. 537) and, where there is one, the Local Women's Development Officer (s. 547), with the Bangsamoro Women Commission (BAA No. 8) informed.

Make the 4-hour report to the police and social welfare office realistic for island and upland barangays: allow a call or text, and name the nearest Regional Trial Court where there is no family court.
Publish the protocol in the local languages (BLGC s. 67) so desk officers and victims can use it.
barmm.fits: Cities and municipalities enacting for all their barangays, or a sangguniang barangay on its own; suits every part of BARMM.

ordinances.title: The new comprehensive anti-smoking ordinance of Davao City
ordinances.shortTitle: The New Comprehensive Anti-Smoking Ordinance of Davao City
ordinances.summary: This ordinance bans smoking tobacco, e-cigarettes and shisha in public transport, government and company vehicles, workplaces, accommodation and entertainment establishments, enclosed public places, public buildings and public outdoor spaces, except in designated smoking areas. It puts duties on owners, managers and vehicle operators, and it creates an Anti-Smoking Task Force to enforce the ban.
points: A designated smoking area must be open-air with no roof or walls, at least 10 metres from entrances and places where people pass, no larger than 5 square metres, limited to 1 per place, and free of food or drink. It needs a certificate from the Anti-Smoking Task Force.
Establishments must post 8 x 16 inch "Non-Smoking Establishment" signs at entrances, remove ashtrays, brief staff, report violators and not sell cigarettes in non-smoking areas.
Jeepneys, taxis, buses and other vehicles must display "No Smoking" signs of set minimum sizes.
The Anti-Smoking Task Force is chaired by the City Administrator. It inspects places, certifies smoking areas, apprehends violators and recommends closures.
A first-time violator who does not contest may pay ₱500 within 3 days to avoid prosecution, once only, and must attend smoking-cessation counselling.
₱5,000,000 is appropriated for 2012 to 2016.
ordinances.penalties: ₱1,000 or 1 month in jail, ₱2,500 or 2 months, then ₱5,000 or 4 months for a 3rd offence. Business permit cancellation follows a 3rd violation, and minors go to counselling instead.

barmm.why: Smoking and vaping are common in public vehicles, terminals, offices and markets across BARMM, and few LGUs enforce the national smoke-free rules. Davao City's ordinance is the best-known local model, with strict smoking-area standards and a task force. Its 2012 text predates the national vape law.
adopt: The covered places: public transport, government vehicles, workplaces, enclosed public places, public buildings and outdoor spaces, with schools, hospitals and places of worship included
The designated smoking area standards: open-air, at least 10 metres from entrances, no larger than 5 square metres, 1 per place
The duties on owners and vehicle operators to post signs, remove ashtrays and report violators
The ₱500 no-contest payment for first-time offenders, once only, with cessation counselling and referral of minors to the social welfare officer
change: Re-cite the legal basis to BLGC s. 17 (health and general welfare) and keep RA 9211 as the national law. Check the e-cigarette and shisha rules against the 2022 national vape law (RA 11900), which came after this text

Chair the task force with the administrator, and have the health officer co-chair; both posts are mandatory in BARMM municipalities under BLGC s. 481. Send minors to the social welfare officer under BLGC s. 537
Keep jail terms within BLGC s. 489 for municipalities (6 months) and s. 509 for cities (1 year); Davao's 4-month maximum fits both
Replace the ₱5,000,000 appropriation for 2012 to 2016 with a current amount, and post and publish the ordinance under BLGC s. 571
Add the transport common in the region, such as passenger boats, ferries and terminals in Tawi-Tawi and Basilan, and motorcycles for hire
barmm.fits: Cities and capital towns with terminals and busy public buildings, such as Cotabato City, Marawi, Lamitan and Bongao.

ordinances.title: Providing for an ecological solid waste management, prohibiting certain acts and providing penalties for violations, and for other purposes
ordinances.shortTitle: Davao City Ecological Solid Waste Management Ordinance of 2009
ordinances.summary: This is Davao City's solid waste ordinance under RA 9003. It covers plastic bag and styrofoam limits, waste segregation and collection, composting, materials recovery and disposal. It requires certain establishments to hold a yearly Solid Waste Management Certificate, and it sets up an enforcement unit under the City ENRO with deputised community enforcers.
points: Stores and ambulant vendors may give out only paper, biodegradable, reusable or indigenous-material bags, or used boxes. Non-biodegradable plastic bags and styrofoam food containers are banned 2 years after approval.
Segregation at source is mandatory, and the city collects segregated waste on a schedule. Barangays, households and establishments must compost.
Industrial, agro-industrial and agricultural establishments and institutions such as schools, hospitals and clinics must secure a Solid Waste Management Certificate every year.
Bans littering, open burning, dumping outside the city disposal facility, and mixing health-care or hazardous waste with municipal waste.
The barangay whose enforcer catches a violator keeps 50% of the fine, and 50% of household garbage fees.
₱1,000,000 is appropriated on effectivity.
ordinances.penalties: ₱300 to ₱1,000 or 1 to 15 days of community service or jail for minor acts, up to ₱2,000 to ₱5,000 or 1 to 6 months in jail for the gravest. Business permits are suspended or cancelled from the 4th offence.
ordinances.caveat: One penalty tier is printed inconsistently ("Three Thousand Pesos (P2,000.00)"), and the date of mayoral approval is unclear in the scan.

barmm.why: Urban waste is outgrowing open dumps in Cotabato City, Marawi, Lamitan and growing towns such as Parang and Bongao. Plastic and styrofoam clog drainage in flood-prone areas along the Rio Grande de Mindanao and wash into Lake Lanao and the sea. Davao's ordinance follows RA 9003, a national law that applies in BARMM, so its structure carries over with mostly renaming and re-citing.
adopt: Mandatory segregation at source with scheduled collection of segregated waste, and composting by barangays, households and establishments
The phased ban on non-biodegradable plastic bags and styrofoam food containers, with a 2-year lead time
The yearly Solid Waste Management Certificate for industries, schools, hospitals and clinics
Deputised community enforcers, with 50% of fines going to the barangay that caught the violator
change: Re-cite the basis to national law (RA 9003, as amended by RA 11898 on extended producer responsibility) and to BLGC s. 480, which gives municipalities the solid waste board, plan and materials recovery facility. Cities hold those powers too under BLGC s. 496
Give barangays their segregation and materials recovery duties under BLGC s. 408, and have the province chair the provincial solid waste board under BLGC s. 512
Keep city penalties within ₱5,000 and 1 year (BLGC s. 509). A municipality must cap jail at 6 months (BLGC s. 489). Correct Davao's misprinted tier ('Three Thousand Pesos (P2,000.00)')

Scale the ₱1,000,000 start-up fund and the enforcement unit to the LGU's income. Give small towns a longer plastic phase-out for market and sari-sari vendors so they have time to switch to alternatives
barmm.fits: Cities (Cotabato City, Marawi, Lamitan) and fast-growing municipal centres such as Parang, Datu Odin Sinsuat and Bongao.

ordinances.title: Watershed protection, conservation and management ordinance hereinafter referred to as the Watershed Code
ordinances.shortTitle: Watershed Code
ordinances.summary: Davao City's Watershed Code protects the watersheds that recharge the city's drinking-water aquifers. It declares conservation and agro-forestry areas environmentally critical and bans a list of activities in them, and it regulates plantations in prime agricultural areas. It creates city and barangay bodies to monitor compliance and funds them through an environmental tax.
points: Declares 34,254 hectares of conservation areas and 12,240 hectares of agro-forestry/non-tillage areas environmentally critical, based on the city's Terrain Analysis Study
Conservation areas: bans land conversion, quarrying, water drilling except for household use, structures and businesses, and hunting or motorized equipment without a council permit
Agro-forestry areas: bans aerial spraying and inorganic farm inputs, and phases out monocrop plantations within 3 years, with no new permits or expansion
Plantations in prime agricultural areas must keep a 40-metre buffer from water sources and critical areas, and a 30-metre buffer from homes, schools and chapels
Creates a Watershed Management Council under the Mayor, Watershed Multipartite Monitoring Teams and a Barangay Watershed Management Council in each covered barangay
₱5,000,000 initial fund, plus an annual environmental tax of ₱0.25 per square metre on undertakings of at least 50 hectares
ordinances.penalties: Up to 1 year in jail or a fine of up to ₱5,000, or both; corporations pay an added ₱5,000 and their officers are liable

barmm.why: BARMM's water and power depend on watersheds under pressure: the Lake Lanao basin that feeds the Agus hydro plants, the uplands draining into the Liguasan Marsh, and the Basilan and Upi forests losing cover to logging and plantations. This code shows a city mapping its critical areas, banning conversion and quarrying there, buffering plantations and funding monitoring. Some parts were legally risky even in Davao and should not be copied.
adopt: Declaring conservation and agro-forestry zones from a terrain or hazard study, with a ban list for each zone
Buffers of 40 metres from water sources and 30 metres from homes, schools and places of worship
A watershed council plus barangay watershed councils and multipartite monitoring teams
Recognition that ancestral domain rights under IPRA must be respected inside covered areas
change: Base the code on BLGC s. 17 and s. 538, which tasks the ENRO with protecting watersheds, and require the sanggunian's prior approval for projects that threaten forest cover under BLGC s. 32

Drop or rewrite the outright aerial spraying ban: the Supreme Court struck down Davao City's separate aerial spraying ban in 2016 (Mosqueda v. Pilipino Banana Growers), so a copy invites the same challenge
Treat the ₱0.25 per square metre environmental tax as a new tax under BLGC s. 211, with a prior public hearing, and publish it under BLGC s. 213

Bring ancestral domain areas of the Teduray, Lambangian and Dulangan Manobo under BAA No. 64 and IPRA (national law), with consent of the affected communities, and seat IP representatives as BLGC s. 132 requires
Keep penalties within the city cap in BLGC s. 509 (₱5,000 or 1 year) or the municipal cap in BLGC s. 489; the added ₱5,000 on corporations pushes past it
barmm.fits: Cities and upland municipalities above water sources: Marawi and the Lake Lanao towns, Upi, South Upi and West Upi, and the Basilan interior.

ordinances.title: Regulating the tourism industry in the City of Davao
ordinances.shortTitle: The Tourism Development Code of Davao City
ordinances.summary: This is a tourism code. It requires every tourism-related business in Davao City to register with the City Tourism Office and sets standards by type of business: accommodation, resorts, restaurants, tourist land and sea transport, malls, recreation, museums, homestays, events organisers, medical tourism and wellness, entertainment, theme parks, convention centres and marinas. It also covers inspections, upgrading and downgrading, and fines.
points: No tourism business may operate without a certificate of registration from the City Tourism Office and a Mayor's permit. The registration fee is paid once, unless the business stops operating for 6 months or loses its permit.
Accommodation establishments and resorts are classified and inspected every year. They must keep guest registers and submit tourist arrival reports.
An establishment that fails to fix defects found in inspection faces an administrative fine of ₱1,000 up to ₱5,000, then suspension or revocation of its registration.
Tourist sea transport (pumpboats) needs a certificate of public conveyance and seaworthiness from MARINA or the Coast Guard, plus a city accreditation valid for 1 year.
Resorts must provide lifeguards, security, medical services and fire-fighting equipment.
ordinances.penalties: Licensees: at least 6 months in jail or a ₱5,000 fine, or both, and the license is revoked. Unlicensed operators: at least 1 year in jail or ₱2,000 to ₱5,000. The Mayor may also impose administrative fines of ₱1,000 to ₱5,000.
ordinances.caveat: The OCR prints the number inconsistently (the first page reads "Series of 2007" and some page headers read "328-07"). The city legal office endorsement and the 8 December 2009 enactment confirm 0328-09, and it was approved on 6 April 2010.

barmm.why: Tourism is growing in BARMM, from the islands and heritage mosques of Tawi-Tawi to Lake Lanao and the Blue Lagoon in Datu Odin Sinsuat, but resorts, homestays and boat operators are mostly unregistered and uninspected. Davao City's code shows how to register, classify and inspect them. Much of it, though, covers malls, theme parks, medical tourism and marinas that few BARMM LGUs have, and its penalties go past BLGC limits.
adopt: Registration of every tourism business with the tourism office, paid once unless the business stops for 6 months or loses its permit
Yearly classification and inspection of accommodation and resorts, with guest registers and tourist arrival reports
Lifeguards, security, first aid and fire-fighting equipment at resorts
Pumpboat rules: a MARINA or Coast Guard seaworthiness certificate plus a 1-year local accreditation
change: Name the tourism officer under BLGC s. 546, mandatory for provinces and for cities or municipalities with major tourism industries
Fold registration into the business permit process and one-stop shop under BLGC s. 151 rather than a separate office visit

Fix the penalties: 'not less than 1 year' in jail for unlicensed operators exceeds the 1-year ceiling for a city (BLGC s. 509) and the 6-month ceiling for a municipality (BLGC s. 489); keep the ₱1,000 to ₱5,000 administrative fines
Cut the categories you do not have (malls, theme parks, medical tourism, convention centres, marinas) and add homestays, island-hopping operators and heritage sites

Add Muslim-friendly standards such as prayer spaces and clear halal labelling, but do not require every restaurant to be halal; keep national accreditation by the Department of Tourism under the national Tourism Act (RA 9593)
barmm.fits: Coastal and lake municipalities with resorts and boat tours: Bongao and the Tawi-Tawi islands, Basilan's coast, Lake Lanao towns and Datu Odin Sinsuat.

ordinances.title: Providing mandatory representation for Indigenous Peoples in the City Council of Davao and providing funds therefor
ordinances.shortTitle: Indigenous Peoples mandatory representation ordinance
ordinances.summary: Gives Davao City's Indigenous Peoples a mandatory representative in the City Council, as allowed by the Local Government Code and the IPRA. The seat rotates each term among the city's 6 major IP groups. The representative has the same pay, powers and privileges as other council members.
points: The seat rotates per term among the Ata, Kalagan, K'lata, Matigsalog, Tagabawa and Ubo Manubo, in that order
The Mayor creates a Technical Working Group under RA 8371 and NCIP rules to design the selection process, subject to council approval
The representative serves 3 years
Pay, benefits, powers and duties equal those of regular council members, with a focus on the collective interest of IPs
Funds are appropriated every year from the General Fund
ordinances.caveat: The Mayor did not sign it; the text records it as deemed approved after the period for her action lapsed.

barmm.why: Teduray, Lambangian, Dulangan Manobo and other non-Moro Indigenous Peoples live in Maguindanao del Norte and del Sur, the SGA and parts of Lanao del Sur, often as a minority in their LGU. Davao's idea of rotating the seat among several groups, so no single group monopolises it, helps where more than one IP community lives in the same LGU. But in BARMM the seat comes from the BLGC itself, so the ordinance becomes an implementing one, not the source of the right.
adopt: The rotation of the seat per term among the LGU's IP groups, where the groups themselves agree to it
Equal pay, benefits, powers and duties with regular sanggunian members, focused on the collective interests of IPs
A yearly appropriation from the general fund
The 3-year term
change: Base it on BLGC s. 132, which guarantees IP representation where IPs are at least 5% of the population but hold no more than 50% of elective offices, or where a native title recognised by MIPA lies in the LGU; for municipalities and barangays, also s. 488 and s. 418.

Replace the NCIP and RA 8371 selection process with the joint MIPA and MILG guidelines that s. 132 requires, following the communities' own customs, and cite BAA No. 64. A mayor-appointed technical working group should not design the selection.
Don't fix the rotation order in the ordinance without the groups' consent; have each community's elders agree on it, or it will be contested.
Add the settler seat under BLGC s. 133 where it applies, and the IP seat on the local development council under s. 119, so both are handled in one measure.
Re-cite the veto and deemed-approval rule to BLGC s. 62 (10 days for a city or municipality).
barmm.fits: Municipalities and barangays with Teduray, Lambangian or Dulangan Manobo communities, such as Upi, South Upi and Datu Blah Sinsuat, and SGA municipalities with IP residents.

ordinances.title: Resorting to Indigenous Peoples' traditional way of conflict resolution, when invoked by disputing IP parties, in an Indigenous Cultural Community in Davao City
ordinances.shortTitle: IP Alternative Dispute Resolution in Davao City
ordinances.summary: This ordinance lets Indigenous Peoples in recognised Indigenous Cultural Communities settle disputes before their Council of Elders under customary law, when both parties choose to. It rests on Section 15 of the IPRA (RA 8371) and Section 399 of the Local Government Code. It also sets how that process links back to the Katarungang Pambarangay.
points: Applies to IP residents of ancestral domain areas in 81 listed barangays across Davao City's districts (per Resolution No. 02199-15), except disputes the law bars from compromise.
Both IP parties must voluntarily invoke the Council of Elders. Customary law may not involve cruel, degrading or inhumane punishment, the death penalty or excessive fines.
Each tribe's own justice system and customary law govern the procedure.
Agreements must be written, signed by the parties and the Council of Elders, and submitted to the Katarungang Pambarangay for confirmation. They then bind the parties.
If the Council of Elders does not act within 15 days, the dispute goes automatically to the Lupong Tagapamayapa.
ordinances.penalties: There are no fines. Barangay officials who refuse to refer a case to the elders face administrative charges, and elders who fail to act are sanctioned under customary law, which the NCIP may enforce.
ordinances.caveat: The enactment date is read from poor OCR ("Bth day of January") and may be off.

barmm.why: Teduray, Lambangian, Dulangan Manobo and other non-Moro Indigenous communities have their own justice systems run by councils of elders. Barangay officials still often route their disputes straight to the lupon. The BLGC already recognises these systems, and this short ordinance supplies the missing steps: who may invoke the elders, how a settlement is recorded and confirmed, and what happens if the elders do not act.
adopt: Both IP parties must choose the Council of Elders voluntarily, and customary law may not use cruel or degrading punishment, the death penalty or excessive fines
Each tribe's own procedure governs, with written agreements signed by the parties and the elders
Settlements are confirmed through the lupon, and a case goes to the lupon automatically if the elders do not act within 15 days
Administrative charges for barangay officials who refuse to refer a case to the elders
change: Replace Section 399 of the 1991 Code with BLGC s. 427, which is stronger: where most barangay residents belong to Indigenous communities, customary proceedings take the place of the katarungang pambarangay. The opt-in model is then needed only in mixed barangays

Replace the NCIP with the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs under BAA No. 64. Build the list of covered barangays from MIPA-recognised ancestral domains or native titles (BLGC s. 132) and any tribal barangays under BLGC s. 406
Spell out the cases that cannot go to settlement under BLGC s. 436, especially violence against women and children, instead of the general 'barred by law' wording
Add the rules on written settlements in a language both parties know (BLGC s. 440) and on a settlement taking effect as a final judgment after 10 days (BLGC s. 445)
Keep this ordinance for non-Moro IP disputes. Handle rido between clans through the ad hoc bodies of the peace and order council under BLGC s. 128, and keep Shari'ah court matters out
barmm.fits: Municipalities and barangays with Teduray, Lambangian and other IP communities, such as Upi, South Upi and West Upi, and tribal barangays.

ordinances.title: Ordinance creating the City Peace 911 Council and Peace 911 sa Barangay, subject to all laws and existing legal rules and regulations
ordinances.shortTitle: City Peace 911 Council ordinance
ordinances.summary: Creates a City Peace 911 Council to advise the city on peacebuilding, and Peace 911 sa Barangay bodies in barangays the Mayor approves. It builds on Davao's Peace 911 programme and the Positive Peace framework, with Peace 911, The Center for Peacebuilding, as secretariat.
points: City council: the Mayor as chair, plus 2 government, 2 private sector, 1 faith-based, 1 education, 1 city councillor and 1 youth member; members are appointed by the Mayor and reconstituted each fiscal year
Barangay body: 1 kagawad, 1 barangay functionary as secretary and 5 sector members, appointed by the Punong Barangay with council concurrence
Farm, fisheries and Indigenous Peoples seats are required in agricultural, coastal and IPMR barangays
Barangay policies need approval by the City Peace 911 Council and adoption by barangay resolution
Both bodies meet at least once a quarter; honoraria are set by the Mayor, subject to funds
Renames the Peace 911 General Committee under Executive Order No. 08, s. 2021; automatic review every 3 years

barmm.verdict: Take the idea, not the text
barmm.why: Davao's council was built around its own Peace 911 programme and centre, which was aimed mainly at the communist insurgency in Paquibato. BARMM's conflicts are different: rido between clans, armed groups, land disputes and the transition of former combatants, in places such as the Maguindanao provinces, Lanao del Sur, Basilan and the SGA. The useful idea is a standing peace council with sector seats and a matching body in each barangay. The rest of the text is too tied to Davao.
adopt: A city or municipal peace council with seats for government, private sector, faith-based, education and youth members, meeting at least quarterly
Matching barangay bodies with a kagawad, a barangay functionary as secretary and sector members
Required farm, fisheries and Indigenous Peoples seats in agricultural, coastal and IP barangays
An automatic review every 3 years
change: Build it as a committee of the peace and order council or as the ad hoc rido body that BLGC s. 128 allows (traditional and religious leaders, women and others trusted by the parties), not as a parallel council under a programme name
Add required seats for women, Indigenous Peoples and settler communities where BLGC s. 132 and s. 133 call for them, and work with the lupon and customary dispute systems recognized in BLGC s. 427
Link the council to the regional transitional justice and reconciliation programme (BAA No. 89) and to displaced families' needs under BAA No. 62

Drop the rule that barangay policies need city council approval. Barangays act by ordinance or resolution under city review (BLGC s. 65), and a council appointed by the mayor should not hold a veto over them
Set honoraria in the ordinance or the budget instead of leaving them to the mayor
barmm.fits: Municipalities with active rido or post-conflict areas in the Maguindanao provinces, Lanao del Sur, Basilan and the SGA.

ordinances.title: Creating the Persons with Disabilities Affairs Center (PDAC) – the Persons with Disabilities Affairs Office (PDAO) of Davao City, as a division under the City Social Welfare and Development Office (CSWDO), determining their duties, powers, and functions
ordinances.shortTitle: An Ordinance Creating the PDAC-PDAO DC
ordinances.summary: Creates Davao City's Persons with Disabilities Affairs Office, required by RA 10070, as a division of the City Social Welfare and Development Office. It sets the division's functions, its 2 sections, 15 plantilla positions with salary grades and qualifications, and requires sign language interpreters on staff.
points: The division is headed by a Disability Affairs Officer IV (SG 22) with a Disability Affairs Officer III (SG 18) as assistant head
Has an Operations Section and a Promotive Section, with 15 regular positions in total
Positions are appointed by the Mayor under Civil Service rules; the head needs 3 years of disability-affairs experience and 16 hours of training
At least 1 administrative officer, 3 promotive-section assistants and 1 staff member per congressional district must interpret sign language
The city must fund the office as required by RA 10070

barmm.why: Many BARMM LGUs have a PDAO on paper or a focal person with no staff, while conflict and poor maternal care leave a large number of persons with disabilities unregistered and unserved. This ordinance is a clean template for creating the office: functions, sections, positions, qualifications and sign language interpreters. The BLGC makes the office mandatory, so the question for most councils is size, not whether.
adopt: The office's functions and its split into an operations section and a promotive section
Qualifications for the head, including 3 years of disability-affairs experience and 16 hours of training
The requirement that some staff interpret Filipino Sign Language (RA 11106, national law)
Appointment by the mayor under civil service rules
change: Re-cite the basis to BLGC s. 480 and s. 481 (mandatory PDAO officer in municipalities; 4th to 6th class towns may name a focal person) or BLGC s. 513 for provinces, alongside RA 10070 (national law)
Size the plantilla to what the LGU can pay: 15 positions at SG 22 and below will not fit most municipalities under the personal services cap in BLGC s. 349 (45% or 55% of regular income)
Fund programs from the 1% for persons with disabilities in BLGC s. 348, and link the office to the council for persons with disabilities in BLGC s. 130
Follow BLGC s. 87 and BAA No. 17 for the staffing pattern, and decide whether the office sits under the MSWDO (as in Davao) or stands alone
barmm.fits: Every province, city and 1st to 3rd class municipality; smaller towns can adopt a 2 to 3 person version.

ordinances.title: Regulating the establishment, classification, administration and operation of government owned/operated public markets in the City of Davao, otherwise known as the "Market Code of Davao City"
ordinances.shortTitle: Market Code of Davao City
ordinances.summary: Davao City's market code governs city-owned and city-operated public markets: their administration, classification, stall rentals and fees, how stalls are leased, and rules for stallholders, sanitation and the slaughterhouse. It applies to stallholders, vendors, market personnel and cargadores in the city's public markets.
points: Classifies markets by average monthly income over the past 3 months: Class A ₱100,000 or more, Class B ₱50,000 to ₱100,000, Class C below ₱50,000
Sets stall rentals per square metre per day by section and class (e.g. meat section ₱5.88, ₱4.70, ₱3.92)
Vacant stalls are posted for at least 10 days and awarded by drawing of lots; lessees must run their stalls personally
Unpaid rent past 15 days (daily payers) or 20 days (monthly payers) is cause to revoke the lease and eject the stallholder
Unpaid occupancy pays 3 times the regular rate, extra space pays double, and late rent carries a 25% penalty plus 14% a year interest
Markets open 2:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m.; stalls may not be used as dwellings; selling fish and meat outside the market is banned; covers slaughter permits and fees
ordinances.penalties: Fine of up to ₱1,000, or up to 6 months in jail, or both, plus lease cancellation and ejectment
ordinances.caveat: The scan's OCR is poor in places, especially the rental rate table, so check figures against the original.

barmm.verdict: Take the idea, not the text
barmm.why: The public market is a main source of own income for most BARMM municipalities, and many run theirs with no written rules on stall awards, rent or arrears. Davao City's code covers all of that, but it dates from 1989, its rent table is poorly scanned and decades out of date, and its late-payment interest is a problem in a mostly Muslim region.
adopt: Classifying markets by average monthly income, so rents follow what each market earns
Posting vacant stalls for at least 10 days and awarding them by drawing of lots, with lessees required to run their stalls personally
Revoking leases after 15 or 20 days of unpaid rent, and banning the use of stalls as dwellings
Rules on stall sanitation, market hours and slaughter permits
change: Replace the 25% penalty plus 14% a year interest: BLGC s. 153 lets the sanggunian adopt Shari'ah-compliant rules on late payment instead of interest (riba), and any surcharge must stay within BLGC s. 191 (25% plus at most 2% a month, for no more than 36 months)
Set new rents by ordinance under BLGC s. 148 from current costs; do not reuse the 1989 rates
Put the slaughterhouse under the veterinarian (BLGC s. 543) and require halal slaughter practice in line with local religious authorities

Soften the ban on selling fish and meat outside the market: it hits small fishers, and BLGC s. 156 bars taxing aquatic and farm products sold by marginal fishers and farmers; allow designated landing and trading areas
Keep penalties within ₱5,000 and 6 months for a municipality (BLGC s. 489); use BLGC s. 24 for night markets and street closures
barmm.fits: Municipalities and cities running a public market: Cotabato City, Marawi, Bongao, Lamitan, Parang and the poblaciones of Maguindanao del Sur.

ordinances.title: Establishing and strengthening the City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Volunteer Corps (CDRRMVC) and the Barangay Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Volunteer Corps (BDRRMVC) in Davao City, defining its composition, functions, trainings, support mechanisms, and for other purposes
ordinances.shortTitle: Davao City DRRM Volunteer Corps Ordinance of 2025
ordinances.summary: Creates city and barangay disaster volunteer corps under the City DRRM Office and each barangay DRRM committee. It sets how volunteers and volunteer organizations are accredited, mobilised, insured and supported before, during and after disasters, following RA 10121 and NDRRMC guidelines.
points: The City DRRM Office accredits all volunteers and volunteer organizations and keeps a database of them
Barangay corps are organised by the barangay DRRM committee, with a volunteer coordinator named by the Punong Barangay and teams for rescue, first aid, relief, education and damage assessment
Volunteer organizations must insure their volunteers for at least ₱100,000 against accident, death, disability and hospitalisation
Deployed volunteers must be equipped and self-sustaining for 72 hours; post-activity reports are due within 7 days
Accredited volunteers get burial aid, free government hospital care for mission injuries, psychosocial support, ID cards and training
Funded from the City DRRM Fund, the General Fund or other sources

barmm.why: In BARMM's floods and evacuations, from Cotabato City and the Liguasan Marsh towns to Marawi and coastal Tawi-Tawi, the first responders are often unpaid neighbours, mosque groups and youth. They get no training, insurance or ID. This ordinance turns them into accredited corps with set teams, insurance and benefits. The accreditation and cost burdens need scaling down for BARMM organisations.
adopt: Barangay volunteer corps with a coordinator named by the punong barangay and teams for rescue, first aid, relief, education and damage assessment
Accreditation of volunteers and organisations by the LGU DRRM office, with a central database
Benefits for accredited volunteers: burial aid, free government hospital care for mission injuries, psychosocial support, ID cards and training
72-hour self-sufficiency on deployment and post-activity reports within 7 days
change: Re-cite: in BARMM the barangay development council acts as the barangay DRRM council (BLGC s. 121), and the sangguniang barangay may form volunteer community brigades (s. 414); RA 10121 and RA 9418 stay as the national law basis.

Don't put the ₱100,000 insurance cost on volunteer organisations; most mosque, youth and women's groups in BARMM cannot pay it. Budget it from the 5% calamity fund in BLGC s. 348, and link it to the insurance system for tanods and peacekeeping teams in s. 587.
Accept registration with regional ministries and BARMM bodies, not only SEC, CDA, DOLE or DSWD, and allow madrasah, mosque and traditional leader groups to accredit.

Add displacement: volunteers support evacuation centres under BAA No. 62 and the IDP councils in BLGC s. 130. Set the 40% women target from s. 129 for the corps too, with women volunteers for women's spaces in evacuation centres.
Name the BARMM coordination line for regional mutual aid instead of the regional DRRM council; check BAA No. 13 for which regional office holds disaster response.
barmm.fits: Cities and flood-prone municipalities with many barangays, such as Cotabato City, Marawi and the Liguasan Marsh towns of Maguindanao del Sur and the SGA.

ordinances.title: Institutionalizing the programs, services, privileges, and benefits for solo parents and their children, appropriating funds thereof and for other purposes pursuant to Republic Act No. 8972, as amended by Republic Act No. 11861, known as the Expanded Solo Parents Welfare Act
ordinances.shortTitle: Solo Parents' Ordinance of Davao City
ordinances.summary: Puts the Expanded Solo Parents Welfare Act into effect in Davao City and adds city-funded benefits for resident solo parents and their children. It sets who qualifies, how to register and get a Solo Parent ID, the discounts and subsidies available, and grounds for losing them. It creates a Solo Parent Division and a Solo Parents' Desk under the City Social Welfare and Development Office.
points: Registered solo parents earning minimum wage or below get a ₱1,000 monthly subsidy and ₱1,000 extra burial aid on top of the city's ₱2,000 when their child dies
10% discounts on basic necessities and medicines (up to ₱5,000 each), school supplies, laboratory and diagnostic fees, restaurant bills and medical bills
10% discount and VAT exemption on baby's milk, diapers, medicines and supplements up to the child's age of 6, for solo parents earning under ₱250,000 a year
Up to 7 working days of paid parental leave a year after 6 months of service, plus flexible work schedules; employers may not discriminate against solo parents
City-wide registration across 182 barangays; the Solo Parent ID is valid for 1 year, and termination of benefits takes effect 30 days after written notice
Solo Parents' Week every last week of April; funded from the city's General Fund

barmm.why: BARMM has many solo parents: widows and wives of combatants from decades of conflict, spouses of overseas workers, and women divorced under Muslim law. Few of them hold a Solo Parent ID or get the benefits of the Expanded Solo Parents Act. Davao's ordinance turns that national law into a city registration system, a desk and a budget line, which is the part BARMM LGUs most often lack.
adopt: Registration through the social welfare office down to the barangays, a Solo Parent ID valid for 1 year, and 30 days' written notice before benefits end
The ₱1,000 monthly subsidy for registered solo parents earning minimum wage or less, which the national law already requires of LGUs
A Solo Parents' Desk, a yearly Solo Parents' Week and a General Fund appropriation
Restating the national discounts, VAT exemptions and anti-discrimination rule, so shops and employers know them
change: Re-cite funding to BLGC s. 348, which lists benefits for solo parents among items that must be funded. Put the desk under the mandatory social welfare officer in BLGC s. 537
A separate Solo Parent Division may break the personal services cap in BLGC s. 349 for 4th to 6th class towns; organise it under BLGC s. 87, or use a desk or focal person

Accept proof of status that fits the region: Shari'ah court decrees, registered divorces under Muslim law, and certifications from imams or MSSD for widows of conflict. Take the DSWD's role from the MSSD, which BLGC s. 512 names for social welfare
Check the parental leave and flexible work rules against the Bangsamoro Labor Code (BAA No. 82) for private employers, and cover the spouses of overseas workers with BAA No. 19
Use the barangay registry in BLGC s. 410 to find solo parents, under its data privacy safeguards
barmm.fits: Every city and municipality; the full version suits cities such as Cotabato City and Marawi, and a desk-only version suits small towns.

ordinances.title: Providing for prevention and intervention mechanisms in protecting children against all forms of sexual abuse and exploitation
ordinances.shortTitle: Anti-Sexual Abuse and Exploitation Against Children Ordinance of Davao City
ordinances.summary: Sets up a city-wide system to prevent and respond to sexual abuse and exploitation of children, including online abuse. It creates a multi-agency committee and assigns specific roles to the information office, DepEd, social welfare, barangay child protection councils, police, media, NCIP, civil society and the CHR. It creates no new penalties and relies on national laws for prosecution.
points: Creates a Committee on Children Protection against Sexual Abuse, chaired by the Special Office for Children's Concern with the CSWDO as vice-chair and 13 member agencies
Creates a city Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) to draw up a local cybersecurity plan against cybersex and child pornography
DepEd must run school-based awareness, referral systems and teacher training on spotting abuse
The CSWDO runs center-based programs, responsible parenting, life-skills training, and rescue, rehabilitation and reintegration of victims
Barangay councils for the protection of children must map high-risk areas and reach far-flung areas
The police Women and Children Protection Desk receives reports and must keep a child-friendly reception area

barmm.why: Online sexual exploitation of children is growing wherever cheap mobile internet meets poverty, and children in evacuation sites and far-flung barangays are especially exposed. Davao's ordinance creates no new crimes. It gives each office a clear job in prevention, referral, rescue and reintegration, and leaves prosecution to national law. That structure carries over to BARMM with mostly renamed offices.
adopt: The multi-agency committee with assigned roles for social welfare, schools, police, media, information office and civil society
School-based awareness, referral systems and teacher training on spotting abuse
Barangay councils for the protection of children mapping high-risk areas and reaching far-flung puroks
A child-friendly reception area at the police Women and Children Protection Desk
change: Seat the committee in the local council for the protection of children (BLGC s. 130), funded from its minimum 1% budget share (BLGC s. 348). Make the social welfare officer the lead under BLGC s. 537, since BARMM LGUs have no Special Office for Children's Concern

Rename the partner offices: the Ministry of Social Services and Development for DSWD, the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education for DepEd (and include madaris under the Education Code, BAA No. 18), the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs for NCIP (BAA No. 64), and add the Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission (BAA No. 4)

Update the legal basis to the national laws now in force, especially RA 11930 (2022) on online sexual abuse of children, alongside RA 7610 and RA 9775. Don't call the local body a 'CICC', which is the name of the national cybercrime centre under RA 10175

Add evacuation centres and displaced families to the risk mapping (BAA No. 62). Decide openly how the code will handle child marriage under national law (RA 11596), consulting Shari'ah court officials and ulama, since this is a live issue in the region
barmm.fits: Cities and larger municipalities with a licensed social worker and police desk; barangay duties suit every barangay with a BCPC.

ordinances.title: An ordinance approving the 2005 Revenue Code of the City of Davao, as amended
ordinances.shortTitle: The 2005 Revenue Code of the City of Davao
ordinances.summary: Davao City's full revenue code, governing the levy, assessment and collection of every city tax, fee and charge. It runs 434 sections across 10 chapters: city taxes, permit and regulatory fees, service fees, city charges, the community tax, administrative provisions and remedies, and penalties. It is a complete model for a city council writing or updating its own revenue code under the Local Government Code.
points: Real property tax of 1.5% of assessed value plus 1% for the Special Education Fund, payable in 4 quarterly instalments, with a 10% discount for on-time payment and 20% for full payment before the end of the first quarter.
Idle land tax of 25% of 1% of assessed value, and a real property transfer tax of 80% of 1% of the consideration or fair market value, whichever is higher.
Graduated business tax schedules by gross sales (manufacturers, wholesalers and others), and a franchise tax of 82% of 1% of gross annual receipts.
Amusement tax on admissions: 30% for foreign films and cockpits, 15% for local films, concert halls, KTV clubs, theme parks and stadia, 5% for other amusement places.
Late payment draws a 25% surcharge and interest of up to 2% a month, capped at 36 months; the council may adjust rates once every 5 years by no more than 10%.
Long schedules of permit fees (mayor's permit, building, electrical, sign, zoning, tricycles, cockpits) and charges (garbage collection, parking, hospital, cemetery, slaughter).
ordinances.penalties: Violations not otherwise penalised draw a fine of ₱1,000 to ₱5,000, or 1 to 6 months in jail, or both, without relief from the tax due.
ordinances.amends: Repeals all ordinances, rules and regulations inconsistent with it; no specific ordinance named.

barmm.why: BARMM's cities, especially Cotabato City and Marawi, need a complete city revenue code that covers real property, business, transfer, franchise and amusement taxes and the long schedule of fees and charges. Davao's 434-section code is the most complete model in the library. But several of its rates exceed what the BLGC allows, and parts of it (cockpits, KTV, interest) clash with BARMM law or local values.
adopt: The 10-chapter structure and the long schedules of permit fees and charges as a checklist
Real property tax of 1.5% plus 1% for the Special Education Fund, in 4 quarterly instalments, within BLGC s. 258, s. 261 and s. 276
The 10% on-time and 20% advance-payment discounts, within the 20% cap in BLGC s. 277
The clause that fines do not excuse the tax due
change: Cut the amusement tax: BLGC s. 164 caps it at 10% of gross receipts, and BLGC s. 174 bars cities from exceeding that cap, so the 30% and 15% rates cannot be copied

Recompute the transfer tax (80% of 1%) and franchise tax (82% of 1%) from the base in BLGC s. 158 and s. 160 (50% of 1%) and the 50% city mark-up in BLGC s. 174; Davao's rates include past adjustments a new BARMM code cannot start from

Replace the interest provisions with a Shari'ah-compliant rule if the council chooses, under BLGC s. 153, and add the BARMM exemptions in BLGC s. 259 (mosques, madaris) and s. 260 (displaced owners' property, which matters in Marawi)
Raise the tax penal clause to BLGC s. 576 (₱40,000 to ₱1,200,000 and 1 to 6 months); keep the ₱5,000 and 1 year cap in BLGC s. 509 for non-tax violations
Drop or rethink the cockpit, KTV and similar fee schedules, which many BARMM councils will not license, and hold the public hearings in BLGC s. 212 before enactment
barmm.fits: Cities: Cotabato City, Marawi and Lamitan; provinces can borrow the real property tax chapters.

ordinances.title: Ordinance to provide additional area of one-half hectare out of the city-owned public cemetery at Ma-a, for the exclusive use of the Muslim community as burial site in Davao City and appropriating funds for the construction of its perimeter fence
ordinances.shortTitle: Muslim burial site ordinance
ordinances.summary: Sets aside an extra half hectare of the city-owned public cemetery at Ma-a as a burial site for the exclusive use of Davao City's Muslims. It funds a perimeter fence and related development, citing the general welfare clause and the state's duty to provide a decent burial site.
points: Reserves an additional 5,000 sq m of the Ma-a public cemetery for Muslim burials
Appropriates ₱4,100,000 for the perimeter fence and other development of the area
Takes effect on approval and publication in a local newspaper 3 consecutive times

barmm.why: A burial site set aside for one faith community is a simple, 2-page ordinance any council can pass. In BARMM the need often runs the other way: Muslim-majority towns may need sites for Christian, Teduray or Lambangian families, while Cotabato City and the SGA municipalities may need more room for Muslim burials, which happen within a day of death.
adopt: Reserving a defined area of a public cemetery for the exclusive use of one community
A fixed appropriation for the perimeter fence and site development
The general welfare basis and a short, plain structure
change: Re-cite the basis to the general welfare clause (BLGC s. 17) and the municipal duty to provide public cemeteries (BLGC s. 480)
Replace 'publication 3 times in a newspaper' with the BLGC rule: effect 10 days after posting at the hall and 2 other conspicuous places (BLGC s. 67)
If new land is needed, follow BLGC s. 22 on expropriation; a non-profit cemetery is exempt from real property tax under BLGC s. 259

For Indigenous burial grounds, consult the community and the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs under BAA No. 64; for Muslim sites, consult local ulama on layout and qibla orientation, and check flood risk and the national Sanitation Code
barmm.fits: Cotabato City, SGA municipalities and mixed towns in Maguindanao del Sur and Basilan where more than one faith community shares the public cemetery.
